title: Why life lives where it does: moving continents, islands and invasive species

summary.text: Both polar seas are freezing and full of fish, yet penguins live only in the south and polar bears only in the north. Why? In this unit you will place eight animals on a world map, test whether two families of copies that never mix stay alike, and line up fossils on the Gondwana jigsaw.
summary.art: A globe seen from the side with penguins standing on ice at the bottom and a polar bear on ice at the top, and a wide band of warm blue sea between them.

intro.hook: Penguins swim in icy seas and eat fish. The Arctic, at the top of the world, is an icy sea full of fish. So why does no penguin live in the Arctic?
intro.text: The Arctic would probably suit a penguin. But penguins first lived in the far south, and nearly all of them still do. Between the south and the Arctic lie thousands of kilometres of warm sea, and penguins need cold water. Polar bears have the same problem the other way round. Their ancestors were bears of the north, and no bear ever walked to Antarctica. So there are two questions to ask about any living being. Does this place suit her? And could her ancestors get here? The study of where living beings are found, and why, is called biogeography. In this unit you find the barriers that keep living beings apart. You learn that the continents themselves move. And you test what happens when one family is split in two.
intro.art: A penguin standing on an ice edge looking north across a warm tropical sea, with a small polar bear far away at the top of a curved Earth.

outcomes: By the end I can give three reasons why a living being is found in one place and not in another.
By the end I can name barriers that stop living beings spreading, and four ways of crossing them.
By the end I can explain how moving continents carried living beings apart, and tell the story of India's journey.
By the end I can explain why a shallow sea became a land bridge in the ice age and a deep sea did not.
By the end I can explain why groups that are kept apart become different, and why islands have endemic species.
By the end I can tell native, introduced and invasive species apart, with examples from India.
By the end I can give reasons why some introduced species spread so fast, and compare ways of controlling them.
By the end I can use fossils, maps, DNA or a fair test as evidence for where a living being came from.

terms.meaning: Biogeography is the study of where living beings are found, and why they are found there.
terms.example: A biogeographer asks why tigers live in Asia but not in Africa, though both have forests and deer or antelope.
terms.art: A world map with small drawings of a tiger on Asia, a kangaroo on Australia and a lemur on Madagascar.

terms.meaning: The range of a kind of living being is the whole area where they live in the wild.
terms.example: The range of the Nilgiri tahr, a mountain goat, is a few high hills in Tamil Nadu and Kerala.
terms.art: A map of South India with one small shaded patch on the hills and a mountain goat drawn beside the patch.

terms.meaning: A barrier is anything that stops a living being from spreading further, such as a sea, a mountain range, a desert or a change in climate.
terms.example: The salty sea is a barrier for a frog. A strip of dry land is a barrier for a river fish.
terms.art: A frog sitting at the edge of the sea and a fish at the edge of a pond, each looking across at land they cannot reach.

terms.meaning: Dispersal is the movement of living beings, or their seeds, eggs or young, from the place where they were born to a new place.
terms.example: A coconut that floats from one beach to another has dispersed.
terms.art: A coconut floating on a wave between two sandy shores.

terms.meaning: A tectonic plate is one of about a dozen huge slabs of rock that together make the hard outer shell of the Earth. The plates carry the continents and the sea floor.
terms.example: India, Sri Lanka and part of the Indian Ocean floor ride on the Indian plate.
terms.art: The Earth drawn like a cracked eggshell, with the piece carrying India coloured in.

terms.meaning: Plate tectonics is the slow movement of the Earth's plates. They move a few centimetres a year, about as fast as a fingernail grows.
terms.example: The Indian plate moves north-east about 5 centimetres every year, and this pushes the Himalaya up.
terms.art: A side view of one slab of rock pushing against another, with mountains crumpling up where they meet.

terms.meaning: Gondwana was a giant southern land that existed long ago. It broke into Africa, South America, Antarctica, Australia, Madagascar and India.
terms.example: Fossils of the same plants are found in India and in Antarctica, because both were once parts of Gondwana.
terms.art: A single large landmass made of Africa, South America, India, Antarctica and Australia fitted together like jigsaw pieces.

terms.meaning: A fossil is what is left of a living being from long ago, kept in rock. It can be a bone, a shell, a leaf print or a footprint.
terms.example: Fossil leaves of a plant called Glossopteris are found in the coal of Jharkhand and Odisha.
terms.art: A flat piece of dark rock split open to show the print of a tongue-shaped leaf.

terms.meaning: A land bridge is a strip of land that joins two larger lands for a time, so that animals and plants can cross on foot or by root.
terms.example: During the last ice age the sea was lower, and dry land joined Sri Lanka to India.
terms.art: A map of the southern tip of India joined to Sri Lanka by a strip of dry land, with deer walking across.

terms.meaning: An ice age is a long cold time when much of the Earth's water is frozen into thick ice on the land. With so much water held in ice, the sea level is lower.
terms.example: About 20,000 years ago the sea was about 120 metres lower than it is today.
terms.art: A coast drawn twice: once with the sea high, and once with the sea low and a wide strip of new dry land.

terms.meaning: A group of living beings is isolated when a barrier keeps them from meeting and having young with others of their kind.
terms.example: Frogs on an island far out at sea are isolated from frogs on the mainland.
terms.art: A small island with a few frogs on it, and a mainland far away across the water with more frogs.

terms.meaning: An ancestor is a living being from long ago from whom later ones are descended, like a great-great-grandparent many times over.
terms.example: The purple frog of Kerala and some tiny frogs of the Seychelles islands share an ancestor who lived on Gondwana.
terms.art: A family tree with one frog at the bottom and two different frogs at the tips of two branches.

terms.meaning: A kind of living being is endemic to a place when they live there naturally and nowhere else on Earth.
terms.example: The Nicobar megapode, a bird who warms her eggs in a mound of sand and leaves, is endemic to the Nicobar Islands.
terms.art: A brown ground bird beside a large mound of sand and leaves at the edge of an island forest.

terms.meaning: A kind of living being is native to a place if they reached it, or arose there, without being carried by people.
terms.example: The neem tree and the tiger are native to India.
terms.art: A neem tree with a tiger resting in the shade under the branches.

terms.meaning: A kind of living being is introduced to a place if people brought them there, on purpose or by accident.
terms.example: The chilli plant was introduced to India from the Americas about 500 years ago.
terms.art: A sailing ship unloading sacks at an old Indian port, with red chillies spilling from one sack.

terms.meaning: An introduced kind of living being is invasive if they spread fast without help and harm the living beings who were there before.
terms.example: Lantana, a garden shrub from tropical America, is invasive in India's forests.
terms.art: A forest floor covered by a tangle of bushes with small pink and yellow flowers, and a deer with nowhere to graze.

terms.meaning: A natural enemy of a living being is another being who eats them, lives on them or makes them ill, and so keeps their numbers down.
terms.example: A tiny weevil who eats only the water fern salvinia is a natural enemy of salvinia.
terms.art: A tiny black beetle with a long snout sitting on a furry green floating leaf.

terms.meaning: Biological control is the use of a natural enemy to bring down the numbers of an invasive plant or animal.
terms.example: In Kerala in the 1980s, weevils from Brazil were released to control salvinia, a water fern from Brazil.
terms.art: A scientist tipping a jar of tiny beetles onto a mat of floating green plants in a canal.

terms.meaning: Every living being carries instructions called DNA and copies them for their young. A mutation is a small mistake in a copy. It is then passed on to the next copies.
terms.example: Every child is born with a few dozen small changes in their DNA that neither parent had.
terms.art: Two long strips of coloured beads side by side, the same except for one bead of a different colour.

explanations.concept: Biogeography: three reasons a living being lives where she does
explanations.definition: A kind of living being is found in a place for three reasons together. The place suits them. Their ancestors could reach it. And the land has a history that took them there or kept them there.
explanations.description: Most people stop at the first reason. They say a camel lives in the desert because the desert suits her. That is true, but it leaves a lot unexplained. The deserts of Australia would suit camels too, and no camel lived there until people brought them in the 1800s. Today hundreds of thousands of camels live wild in Australia. So the Australian desert suited camels all along. Camels were missing only because their ancestors, who lived in Asia and Africa, could not cross the sea. The third reason is the oldest. Land moves, seas rise and fall, and mountains grow. A living being may be where she is because the ground under her ancestors carried them there.
examples: Penguins would probably find food in the Arctic. They are not there, because warm seas lie between.
Wallabies, who are small relatives of kangaroos, were taken from Australia to New Zealand in the 1870s. Their descendants now live wild over a wide area of hill country in the South Island.
Lantana grows very well in India. Yet no lantana grew here until people brought the plant about 200 years ago.
explanations.art: Three small pictures in a row: a camel on sand, a camel looking across a sea, and a continent sliding with animals standing on it.

explanations.concept: Barriers: what stops a living being from spreading
explanations.definition: A barrier is anything that a kind of living being cannot cross in the ordinary course of life.
explanations.description: A barrier is different for each being. The sea stops a frog, because salt water draws the water out through a frog's thin skin. The same sea is a road for a sea turtle. A high, cold mountain range stops a lowland snake and hardly slows an eagle. A desert stops a forest tree, because their seedlings die before they find water. Climate is a barrier too, even where nothing stands in the way. Warm tropical water is a barrier for penguins. So to say what a barrier is, you must also say for whom. This is why two places with the same climate can have quite different animals. The same kinds could live in both. But a barrier lies between, and it has been there for a very long time.
examples: The Himalaya keep many animals of the cold lands to the north apart from the animals of India.
For a fish in a river, dry land and the salty sea are both barriers. So two rivers side by side can hold different fish.
The Palghat Gap is a low, warm, dry break in the cool, wet hills of the Western Ghats. Some hill birds and frogs live on only one side of it.
explanations.art: A row of four barriers, each with a different animal stopped there: a frog at the sea, a snake at a snowy mountain, a tree seed at a desert, a penguin at warm water.

explanations.concept: Crossing a barrier: flying, floating, rafting and riding
explanations.definition: Dispersal is movement to a new place. Living beings cross barriers by flying, by floating, by riding on something that floats, or by riding on another animal.
explanations.description: In 1883 the volcano Krakatau in Indonesia exploded and destroyed most of the island. When scientists landed nine months later, the only living being they found was one spider. A young spider can let out a thread of silk and be carried by the wind. Within a few years grasses and ferns were growing, from seeds and spores brought by wind, sea and birds. Larger animals cross water on rafts, which are mats of plants or fallen trees washed out to sea. In 1995, after two hurricanes, at least fifteen iguanas landed on the island of Anguilla in the Caribbean Sea. They had ridden on uprooted trees for about 320 kilometres. A crossing like that is very rare. But a thing that happens once in ten thousand years has happened about a hundred times in a million years. Over a very long time, rare crossings become almost certain.
examples: A coconut has a thick husk full of air and can float in the sea for many weeks.
The ancestors of Madagascar's lemurs probably crossed from Africa on a raft of plants, between 50 and 60 million years ago.
A kind of dragonfly called the globe skimmer flies across the sea between India and East Africa.
explanations.art: A mat of floating branches on the open sea with two green iguanas clinging to it, and a small island on the horizon.

explanations.definition: The hard outer shell of the Earth is broken into about a dozen large plates. The plates move a few centimetres a year, and they carry the continents with them.
explanations.description: Under the plates lies the mantle, a thick layer of hot rock. The rock of the mantle is solid, but it is so hot that it flows very slowly, a little like very stiff dough. Hot rock rises and cooler rock sinks. Where two plates move apart, hot rock comes up and makes new sea floor. Where they meet, one plate may slide down under the other, and its sinking weight pulls the rest of the plate along. Why is the inside of the Earth hot? About half the heat is left over from the time the Earth formed. The other half is made today by atoms of uranium, thorium and potassium deep in the rock. These atoms slowly break down, and each one gives out a little heat. Today satellites measure the movement directly. The Indian plate moves north-east at about 5 centimetres a year.
examples: The Atlantic Ocean gets a few centimetres wider every year, as new sea floor forms down its middle.
India pushing into Asia lifts the Himalaya and causes earthquakes from Kashmir to Arunachal Pradesh.
Your fingernails grow about 4 centimetres in a year. That is close to the speed of a plate.
explanations.art: A slice through the Earth showing a thin cracked shell on top of a thick glowing layer with slow curling arrows, and a continent riding on one piece of shell.

explanations.definition: India was once part of Gondwana, a giant southern land. India broke away, moved north across the sea for tens of millions of years, and joined Asia.
explanations.description: About 180 million years ago Gondwana began to break up. India and Madagascar stayed joined for a long time. Then, roughly 90 million years ago, India split from Madagascar. About 65 million years ago the small piece of land that is now the Seychelles islands broke off from India. India was then an island continent, and it moved north unusually fast for a plate. About 50 million years ago India began to push into Asia, and the Himalaya started to rise. Scientists' dates for these events differ by several million years, because they come from different kinds of rock evidence. The name Gondwana comes from India. In 1872 the geologist Henry Medlicott named a set of rock layers in central India after the land of the Gond people. Later the Austrian geologist Eduard Suess used the name for the whole lost southern land.
examples: Fossils of Lystrosaurus, a plant-eating land animal about 1 metre long, are found in India, in South Africa and in Antarctica.
Fossil leaves of the plant Glossopteris are found in India, Australia, Africa, South America and Antarctica.
Very old rocks in eastern Madagascar match very old rocks in south-west India.
explanations.art: Four small maps in a row showing India joined to Madagascar, then alone in the sea, then near Asia, then pressed into Asia with mountains.

explanations.concept: Who rode on India, and who walked in later?
explanations.definition: Scientists agree that India carried living beings from Gondwana and also received many from Asia. They do not agree on how large each share is.
explanations.description: The clearest passenger is the purple frog of the Western Ghats. She lives underground for most of the year. In 2003 S. D. Biju and Franky Bossuyt compared her DNA with that of other frogs. Her closest living relatives are tiny frogs who live only on the Seychelles islands, nearly 3,000 kilometres away across the sea. Frogs do not cross salt water easily. The two families share an ancestor who lived on the land when India and the Seychelles were one. People living in those hills knew the frog long before 2003. What the scientists added was her family tree. But India's journey was hard on its passengers. Around 66 million years ago huge lava flows covered much of the land, and the climate changed as India crossed the equator. Many of India's mammals and birds today, such as tigers, deer and hornbills, have their nearest relatives in South-East Asia.
examples: Caecilians are limbless amphibians who burrow in wet soil. Those of the Western Ghats have relatives in the Seychelles and in Africa.
Tigers have their nearest relatives in the rest of Asia, so their ancestors probably walked into India after it joined Asia.

perspectives.who: Franky Bossuyt of Belgium and S. D. Biju of India, who study frogs
perspectives.explanation: Some old families of frogs and caecilians rode on India from Gondwana. A few of them later spread out of India into the rest of Asia.

perspectives.who: Praveen Karanth, a biologist at the Indian Institute of Science in Bengaluru
perspectives.explanation: Family trees built from DNA suggest that many of India's land animals with backbones arrived from Asia after the two lands met. The old Gondwana passengers are a smaller share.
Fossils from the time when India was an island are rare. Until more are found, nobody can say how many kinds of passengers there were, or how many died on the way.

explanations.art: A plump purple frog with a pointed snout on wet soil, and across a drawn sea a tiny brown frog on a leaf on a small island.

explanations.concept: Why kangaroos live only in and near Australia
explanations.definition: Kangaroos and their close relatives are native only to Australia, New Guinea and nearby islands. Their ancestors were there when deep sea cut that land off from all others.
explanations.description: Kangaroos are marsupials. A marsupial mother gives birth to a very small baby, who finishes growing in a pouch on her belly. Long ago marsupials lived across South America, Antarctica and Australia, which were joined as parts of Gondwana. Antarctica was not yet frozen. Then Australia broke away and moved north by itself, with marsupials on board. For tens of millions of years almost no other land mammals could reach it. Bats flew in, and some rats and mice arrived much later across the island chains. So the marsupials of Australia spread into many ways of living. Some graze like deer, some climb like monkeys, and some dig like moles. Kangaroos are missing from India because of this history. India's grasslands would probably feed them. Their ancestors simply never had a way here.
examples: Tree kangaroos live in the forests of New Guinea, which was joined to Australia by land when the sea was lower.
Opossums are marsupials who still live in South and North America.
Wallabies taken to New Zealand by people in the 1870s now live wild there. So relatives of kangaroos can live outside Australia once they are carried.
explanations.art: A map with Australia drifting away from Antarctica, and small kangaroos, koalas and wombats standing on the moving land.

explanations.concept: Wallace's Line: shallow seas, deep seas and land bridges
explanations.definition: Wallace's Line is a boundary between islands with Asian animals and islands with Australian animals. It follows a channel of deep sea that never became dry land.
explanations.description: Alfred Russel Wallace collected animals on the islands of Indonesia for eight years. In 1859 he wrote about a puzzle. Bali and Lombok are islands only about 35 kilometres apart. Bali has woodpeckers, barbets and other birds of Asia. Lombok has cockatoos and honeyeaters, which are birds of Australia. The answer lies under the water. During the last ice age, so much water was frozen on land that the sea stood about 120 metres lower than today. Shallow sea floor became dry land. Sumatra, Java, Borneo and Bali were joined to Asia, and animals walked across. New Guinea was joined to Australia. But the channel between Bali and Lombok is much deeper than 120 metres. It stayed sea, so walking animals stopped there. India has an example too. The sea between India and Sri Lanka is very shallow. Until about 7,000 years ago, dry land joined them.
examples: Elephants, leopards and sloth bears live in both South India and Sri Lanka. Their ancestors could walk across.
Tigers reached Bali on foot when it was joined to Asia. No tiger ever lived on Lombok.
The line is sharper for mammals than for birds, bats and insects, because many of those can fly across.
explanations.art: A side view of the sea floor between three islands, with a shallow shelf between the first two and a deep trench before the third, and a dotted line showing the lower ice-age sea.

explanations.concept: Groups that are kept apart become different
explanations.definition: When a barrier splits one kind of living being into two groups that can no longer have young together, the two groups slowly become different.
explanations.description: Every living being carries instructions, called DNA, in each cell. Parents copy their DNA for their young. The copying is very good, but a few small mistakes are made every time. These copying mistakes are called mutations. Most do nothing that anyone can see. In one large group, parents come from all parts of the group, so each change is spread around or lost. The group changes slowly, and it changes together. Now put a sea between two halves of the group. Each half goes on making its own copying mistakes, and they are not the same mistakes. Chance decides which ones are kept. Natural selection also works on each half, and the two places are not alike. Nothing mixes the two halves any more. After many thousands of generations they can be so different that they are two species. Scientists use this to measure time. They count the differences in DNA between two species. More differences mean a longer time apart.
examples: The purple frog and her Seychelles relatives have been apart since their lands separated, and they now look nothing alike.
Lions in the Gir forest of Gujarat have been cut off from the lions of Africa for a very long time, and differ from them a little in body and in DNA.
Leopards of India and Sri Lanka were one group until about 7,000 years ago. They still look almost the same.
explanations.art: One group of birds on a single landmass, then the land split by sea into two parts, and the birds on each part drawn with slightly different beaks and colours.

explanations.concept: Islands: few arrive, and those few change
explanations.definition: An island has fewer kinds of living beings than the same area of mainland. The further the island is from the mainland, the fewer kinds reach it, and the more of them are endemic.
explanations.description: An island gets its living beings from somewhere else. Only those who can cross the water arrive. So far islands have many birds, bats, insects, geckos and plants with floating or flying seeds. They have few frogs and few large mammals. In 1967 Robert MacArthur and Edward Wilson put this into a theory. A near island gets more arrivals than a far one. A large island keeps more kinds alive than a small one. Wilson and Daniel Simberloff tested it on tiny mangrove islands off Florida. They removed all the insects and spiders, and watched them return. The islands nearest the shore ended with the most kinds, as the theory said. The few who do reach a far island are then isolated. Their descendants change for thousands of generations without mixing with the mainland. That is how an island comes to have endemic species. A hilltop, a lake and a cave are islands in this sense too. Each is a small patch cut off by land of a different kind.
examples: The Nicobar megapode lives only on the Nicobar Islands. The other megapodes live far away to the east.
The Narcondam hornbill lives on one small island in the Andaman Sea and nowhere else.
The cool, wet hilltops of the Western Ghats have frogs and birds found on only one group of hills.
explanations.art: A mainland with many kinds of animals, a near island with several kinds, and a far island with only a bird, a bat and a gecko.

explanations.definition: A native species reached a place without people. An introduced species was brought by people. An invasive species is an introduced one that spreads without help and harms those who were there before.
explanations.description: People are now the greatest carriers of living beings on Earth. A ship or an aeroplane crosses in a day a barrier that held for millions of years. Many introduced species are welcome. Chilli, potato, tomato, groundnut, papaya, cashew and tapioca all came to India from the Americas. They grow where people plant them and do not spread through forests. A smaller number get away from farms and gardens and live wild. Only a few of those become invasive. But those few can change a whole forest or lake. The words depend on the place. The common myna is native to India. People took mynas to Australia in the 1860s to eat insects in vegetable gardens. There the mynas drive native birds out of their nest holes. The chital, India's spotted deer, is native to the mainland. People also took chital to the Andaman Islands, where they eat so many seedlings that the forest is changing.
examples: Native to India: neem, banyan, peafowl, tiger, black pepper.
Introduced to India and not invasive: chilli, potato, tapioca, cashew, marigold.
Invasive in India: lantana, water hyacinth, parthenium, the giant African snail.
explanations.art: Three baskets in a row labelled native, introduced and invasive, holding a neem twig, a bunch of chillies and a sprig of lantana.

explanations.definition: Lantana, water hyacinth, parthenium and the giant African snail were all brought to India by people in the last 200 years. All four have spread widely.
explanations.description: Lantana is a shrub from tropical America with small pink, orange and yellow flowers. The British brought lantana to India as a garden plant about 200 years ago. Birds eat the berries and drop the seeds. A study in 2020 found lantana in more than 40 of every 100 parts of India's tiger forests. The leaves are poisonous to cattle, and grass cannot grow in lantana's shade. Water hyacinth is a floating plant from South America with pale purple flowers. People brought water hyacinth to Bengal for the flowers. A mat of these plants can double in size in one to two weeks, and the mat blocks light and boats. Parthenium is a weed from tropical America, also called congress grass. Parthenium seeds probably came mixed in with imported grain. The pollen and leaves give many people skin rashes and breathing trouble. The giant African snail is native to East Africa and was brought to India in 1847. An adult can be longer than your hand, and these snails eat a very wide range of plants.
examples: Salvinia, a floating fern from Brazil, once choked the canals and rice fields of Kuttanad in Kerala.
A thorny tree from the Americas was planted for firewood in dry parts of India from 1877. In Tamil Nadu these trees are called seemai karuvelam, and they now cover large areas of dry land.
explanations.art: Four small pictures: a lantana bush, a pond covered with purple-flowered floating plants, a weed with tiny white flowers by a road, and a large brown snail on a leaf.

explanations.concept: Why do some newcomers take over?
explanations.definition: Scientists have several explanations for why a few introduced species spread so fast. Each explanation fits some cases, and none fits all.
explanations.description: Lantana is an ordinary shrub in tropical America, growing there among many other plants. In India the same plant covers whole hillsides. The plant is the same, so the difference must lie in the new place. Scientists have tested four main ideas. They are given below. It is likely that several work together, and that the mix is different for each invader. This matters for what we do. If missing enemies are the cause, bringing one enemy may help. If broken ground is the cause, the answer is to stop breaking the ground.
examples: A study of nearly 500 plants introduced to the United States found far fewer kinds of fungus attacking them there than in their home countries.
Another study compared 72 pairs of native and invasive plants. The invaders were eaten just as much as the natives.
Lantana spreads fastest in forests that have been cut, burned or heavily grazed.

perspectives.who: Ryan Keane and Michael Crawley, ecologists (2002): the missing enemies idea
perspectives.explanation: At home, insects and diseases that feed on a plant keep the numbers down. The plant travels without them. In the new land nobody eats the newcomer, so they can put all their growth into spreading.

perspectives.who: Ragan Callaway and Wendy Ridenour, American ecologists (2004): the new chemicals idea
perspectives.explanation: Some plants release chemicals from their roots or leaves. Their old neighbours are used to these chemicals. The plants of the new land are not, and they grow badly beside the newcomer.

perspectives.who: Many ecologists who study disturbed land
perspectives.explanation: People clear, burn and graze the land, and that opens bare ground. Fast-growing newcomers fill bare ground first. On this view the invader is a sign of the damage as much as a cause of the damage.

perspectives.who: Julie Lockwood and other ecologists (2005): the numbers idea
perspectives.explanation: A species brought many times, in large numbers and to many places has many chances to settle. Garden plants are brought again and again, which is why so many invaders began as garden plants.

explanations.art: A lantana bush drawn twice: at home with caterpillars, beetles and spots of disease on the leaves, and in India with clean, whole leaves.

explanations.concept: Biological control: bringing the missing enemy
explanations.definition: Biological control means finding a natural enemy of an invasive species in the invader's homeland, testing that enemy carefully, and releasing them.
explanations.description: Pulling out an invasive plant by hand works on a small patch. It costs a great deal over a whole district, and the plant grows back from what is left. Poison sprays kill other plants and animals too. Biological control tries a third way. Scientists go to the invader's homeland and look for an insect or a fungus who feeds on that plant and on nothing else. Then comes the most important step. For months or years they offer the insect crops and native plants in closed rooms. Only an insect who starves beside every other plant is released. Kerala has a famous success. A tiny weevil from Brazil was released there in the early 1980s against salvinia, the floating fern. Within a few years the canals of Kuttanad were open again. There are famous failures too. In 1935 people took 102 cane toads to Australia to eat beetles in sugarcane fields. Nobody had tested them properly. The toads did not control the beetles. They multiplied into many millions, and their poison kills native animals who try to eat them.
examples: A beetle from Mexico was released in India in 1984 to eat parthenium. The beetles help in some places, though the weed remains common.
In 1872 nine small Indian mongooses were taken to Jamaica to hunt rats in sugarcane fields. They also ate native birds and lizards.
explanations.art: A scientist in a closed room offering a potted rice plant, a banana leaf and a floating fern to a tiny beetle, who sits only on the fern.

explanations.definition: Scientists and local people disagree about how much effort should go into removing introduced species, and which ones.
explanations.description: Nobody argues for keeping lantana in a tiger forest if the shrubs could be removed easily. The argument is about harder cases. Removing an invader from a large area costs a great deal and often fails. Some newcomers have been in a place for centuries, and other living beings now depend on them. Birds nest in lantana and eat the berries. In the dry districts of Tamil Nadu, many poor families earn money by making charcoal from seemai karuvelam. Courts have ordered these trees to be removed, because they use scarce water. In the hills of Karnataka and Tamil Nadu, people of the Soliga and other forest communities build furniture and life-size elephants from lantana stems. On small islands the case is clearer. Rats, cats and goats carried by ships have wiped out many island birds who had never met a hunting mammal.
examples: Lantana has been in India for about 200 years. Chilli has been here for about 500. Only one of them harms forests.
On many islands, removing introduced rats has let seabirds come back to nest.

perspectives.who: Mark Davis and 18 other ecologists, in the journal Nature (2011)
perspectives.explanation: Judge a species by what they do, and not by where they came from. Most introduced species do little harm, and some help. Spend money only on the ones that cause real damage.

perspectives.who: Daniel Simberloff and 140 other scientists, replying in Nature (2011)
perspectives.explanation: Origin does matter. A newcomer may look harmless for decades and then spread suddenly. By then removal is too late. It is cheaper and safer to stop a newcomer early.

perspectives.who: A family in a dry district of Tamil Nadu who make charcoal from seemai karuvelam
perspectives.explanation: These trees grow where nothing else will, and they are our income in a year without rain. If they are removed, something must replace what they give us.

explanations.art: A life-size elephant made of woven brown stems standing in a forest clearing, with two craftspeople weaving the trunk.

explanations.concept: From atoms deep in the Earth to frogs on islands: is the Earth unusual?
explanations.definition: The Earth is the only planet known to have moving plates. Some scientists think moving plates are needed for a planet to have many kinds of life. This is an idea, and it cannot yet be tested.
explanations.description: Follow the chain from the smallest thing to the largest. Deep in the Earth, atoms of uranium and thorium break down and give out heat. The heat keeps the mantle slowly moving. The moving mantle helps to shift the plates. A plate carried India away from Madagascar. The frogs on the two lands could no longer meet, and over millions of years they became different families. So one reason there are so many kinds of frogs is the heat of atoms far underground. Mars and Venus are rocky planets like the Earth. As far as anyone can tell, their outer shells are single pieces that do not move as plates. Is that connected with the fact that we have found no life there? Nobody knows. We have only one planet with life to study.
examples: Moving plates build mountains, and mountains make rain shadows, cold peaks and isolated valleys. Each is a new kind of place to live.
Volcanoes at plate edges return carbon dioxide to the air. Over millions of years this has helped to keep the Earth from freezing over.

perspectives.who: Peter Ward and Donald Brownlee, American scientists, in the book Rare Earth (2000)
perspectives.explanation: Moving plates keep a planet's climate steady and keep making new, separate places. Without them, animal life might never have become so varied. Such planets may be rare.
We know of one living planet. A planet without moving plates might support life in ways we have not imagined. One example cannot tell us what is needed.

explanations.art: A cut-away Earth with tiny glowing atoms deep inside, arrows rising to a moving plate, and on the surface two small lands drifting apart with a frog on each.

agreed.text: The continents move a few centimetres a year, and they have been joined and separated in the past.
agreed.evidence: Satellites measure the movement directly today. Matching rocks and fossils on separate continents, and the pattern of young rock along the middle of the oceans, show the past movement.
agreed.context: This card is about the movement of the continents, which most scientists doubted a hundred years ago.

agreed.text: India was once joined to Madagascar, Antarctica and Australia, and joined Asia later.
agreed.evidence: The same fossil plants and land animals are found in the rocks of all these lands. The sea floor of the Indian Ocean records India's path north.
agreed.context: This card is about where the land of India used to be.

agreed.text: A kind of living being can be absent from a place that suits them, only because they could not reach it.
agreed.evidence: Camels in Australia, wallabies in New Zealand and lantana in India all live well in lands their ancestors never reached. People carried them.
agreed.context: This card is about why a living being may be missing from a place where she could live.

agreed.text: Groups of one species that are kept apart for long enough become different species.
agreed.evidence: Islands and other isolated places have many endemic species whose nearest relatives live on the nearest mainland. DNA shows how long each pair has been apart.
agreed.context: This card is about what happens to living beings who are separated by a barrier.

agreed.text: Far islands have fewer kinds of living beings than near islands of the same size.
agreed.evidence: Counts on islands all over the world show it. Edward Wilson and Daniel Simberloff also tested it by clearing tiny mangrove islands and watching insects return.
agreed.context: This card is about how the distance of an island from the mainland affects who lives there.

agreed.text: Invasive species are one of the main causes of extinction, most of all on islands.
agreed.evidence: Records of extinct island birds show that many disappeared soon after rats, cats or mongooses arrived with people.
agreed.context: This card is about the harm that some introduced species do.

challenging.claim: Each animal lives in the place that suits them best.
challenging.who: A common way of speaking, and many school books
challenging.for: Animals do fit the places where they live. A camel's body suits a desert and a fish's body suits water.
challenging.against: Many places would suit a species who is not there. Camels were absent from Australia's deserts until people brought them, and now live wild there in very large numbers. Fitting a place and being able to reach it are separate things.
challenging.context: This card is about the common idea that every animal is found wherever the land suits them.

challenging.claim: The continents have always been where they are, and sunken land bridges once joined them.
challenging.for: Nobody could feel the ground move, and nobody knew a force that could shift a continent. A sunken bridge explained why the same fossils lie on both sides of an ocean.
challenging.against: Maps of the sea floor found no sunken bridges. They found a long crack where new sea floor forms. Satellites now measure the continents moving.
challenging.context: This card is about an old explanation for why the same fossils are found on lands far apart.

challenging.claim: Invasive species succeed because they are stronger than native species.
challenging.for: Lantana and water hyacinth do push out native plants wherever they spread.
challenging.against: At home in the Americas, lantana and water hyacinth are ordinary plants that take over nothing. They are the same plants in India. What differs is the place: fewer enemies, more disturbed ground, or neighbours who are not used to them.
challenging.context: This card is about why a plant from another continent can spread over a forest or a lake.

challenging.claim: A natural enemy brought from abroad is always safer than poison sprays.
challenging.who: Some early supporters of biological control
challenging.for: A well-tested enemy attacks only the invader and goes on working for years at no cost. The salvinia weevil in Kerala did exactly that.
challenging.against: A badly tested enemy becomes a new invader. Cane toads in Australia and mongooses in Jamaica harmed native animals and did not solve the first problem.
challenging.context: This card is about controlling an invasive species by releasing an animal who eats them.

challenging.claim: Most of India's animals have been in India since Gondwana.
challenging.who: A popular idea about India as a raft that carried animals from Gondwana
challenging.for: Some old families, such as the purple frog and the caecilians, do have their relatives on other pieces of Gondwana.
challenging.against: DNA family trees show that many of India's mammals, birds and reptiles have their nearest relatives in the rest of Asia. Their ancestors probably arrived after India joined Asia.
challenging.context: This card is about where the ancestors of India's animals came from.

big_questions.q: Lantana has grown in India for 200 years, and chilli for 500. How long must a newcomer stay before we call them native?
big_questions.hint: Tigers probably walked into India after it joined Asia. Is the answer about time, about harm, or about who did the carrying?

big_questions.q: In the Separated Lines Test, nobody tried to make the two families different. So what made them different?
big_questions.hint: Look at what was missing between the two separated families, and present between the two mixed ones.

big_questions.q: People walked and sailed from Africa to every land on Earth, and changed each one. Are humans an invasive species?
big_questions.hint: Use the definition: carried by people, spreads by themselves, harms those who were there before. Which parts fit, and which do not?

big_questions.q: The ground under your home has moved thousands of kilometres. So what do we mean when we say a place stays where it is?
big_questions.hint: A place on a map is fixed by its distance from other places. What happens if all of them are moving?

big_questions.q: A weevil is taken from Brazil to Kerala to eat one fern. Who has the right to decide that?
big_questions.hint: Think of the farmers, the fern, the weevils, the fish under the mat, and the people who will live there in fifty years.

big_questions.q: If a storm had not carried a few monkeys across the sea long ago, South America would have no monkeys. How much of the living world is there by accident?
big_questions.hint: Think about which living beings near you had ancestors who arrived by a rare crossing.

story.title: The Leaf With No Holes
story.note: Ammu, Unni, their father, the tea shop man and the visiting scientist are made up. So are Ammu's leaf count and the ducks who would not eat the fern. These facts are real. Kuttanad in Kerala is a region of canals and rice fields that lie lower than the water around them. A floating fern called salvinia, known in Kerala as African payal, was first recorded in the state in the 1950s. By the 1960s these ferns covered canals and rice fields. The fern really comes from south-eastern Brazil. A weevil from Brazil who feeds only on salvinia was brought to India in 1982 or 1983 and released in Kerala. In 1985 P. J. Joy and three colleagues reported that the weevils had controlled the fern in Kuttanad. Such insects are tested on crops in closed cages before they are released.
text: In Kuttanad the water is higher than the fields. Mud walls hold the canals up, and the rice grows below them, lower than the fish. Ammu was ten. She had crossed the canal to school in the family's small boat every day since she was six.

That year the crossing took twice as long. A green mat lay over the water from bank to bank. People called the plants African payal. Each one was no bigger than her palm, a little raft of soft, furry leaves folded like the pages of a book. But there were so many that the pole stuck fast in them. Her brother Unni had to lean over the front and push them aside with a coconut frond.

Every Sunday the men of the ward stood in the canal up to their chests and dragged the payal out with rakes. They piled the plants on the bank in heaps as high as the tea shop. By the next Sunday the water was green again.
"They are stronger than we are," said the tea shop man. Everyone agreed.
Ammu did not know whether the payal were strong. She only thought they were strange, and she found out why because of the ducks.
Her job after school was to walk the family's ducks down to the water. Ducks will eat almost anything green. They swam through the payal as if through thick porridge, and ate none.

One evening, while she waited for them, she picked a water lily leaf to fan herself. The leaf had three holes in it, and a thin brown track where something small had tunnelled. She looked at the taro on the bank. The edges of the leaves were chewed. A caterpillar had rolled up inside a banana leaf. As for the rice, her father complained every single year about who was eating the crop.
Then she scooped up a handful of payal and turned the plants over, one after another. Not a hole. Not a bite. She tried twenty. Unni counted fifty more out of the boat. Every leaf was whole.
"Everyone here gets eaten by somebody," she told Unni. "Except these."
"Maybe they taste bad," said Unni.
"Karela tastes bad. Somebody still eats Amma's karela plants."
Unni had no answer, and neither had she. It bothered her for a week.

In the week before Onam, a jeep came along the bund road, which did not happen often. A woman in a cotton sari and rubber boots got out. She carried a glass jar with a cloth tied over the top. She was from the agricultural university at Thrissur, and the ward member had called everyone to the tea shop to hear her. Ammu was sent to fetch her father, and she stayed at the back.
The jar went from hand to hand. Inside were a few wet payal and a scattering of black specks, each one smaller than a grain of rice. The specks had legs.
"Weevils," said the woman. "A kind of beetle. We would like to put them in your canal."
The tea shop man laughed so much that he had to sit down. "Madam, we have pulled out forty lorry-loads. You have brought us a spoonful of insects."
"Do they eat the payal?"
The words were out before Ammu could stop them. People turned round.
"Nobody eats the payal," she said, more quietly. "I looked. The lily has holes, and the taro has holes. The payal have none. Not one."
The woman looked at her for a moment. Then she smiled, as if Ammu had handed her something. "Come to the front and say that again."
Ammu said it again.

"She is right, and that is the whole trouble," the woman said. "You call these plants African, but they come from Brazil, on the other side of the world. In Brazil they grow in quiet corners of rivers, a patch here and a patch there. Nobody there rakes them out. These weevils do the work. The grown ones eat the buds, and their young bore into the stems. When the payal were brought to our country, the weevils were left behind. For thirty years the payal have lived here with nobody to eat them."
"So they are not strong," Ammu said slowly. "They only came without their eaters."
"Yes. So we went back and fetched the eaters."
Ammu's father asked what every farmer there wanted to ask. "And when they have finished the payal? Will they start on my rice?"

"That was tested before anything else," said the woman. "For months these weevils were kept in closed cages with rice, with banana, with taro and with coconut seedlings, and no payal. They starved beside the rice. They eat this one plant. When the payal go, most of the weevils go too."
They tipped the jar out beside the boat steps. The specks crawled down among the furry leaves and were gone.

For a month nothing changed. For two months nothing changed, and the tea shop man said so every day. The Sunday raking went on. Each evening, while the ducks fed, Ammu turned the payal over and found whole leaves, whole leaves, whole leaves.

It was Unni who found the first one, in the hot weeks before the rains. The bud in the middle had gone brown, and in the stem was a hole as fine as a pinprick. After that they found them everywhere near the steps. The brown plants filled with water and grew heavy. One by one they sank.
By the next Onam a strip of open water ran down the middle of the canal, wide enough for two boats. It stayed open without a single rake.
Some payal still floated along the edges. Ammu lifted one out as the boat went by, and looked underneath. There was a small, neat hole.
She showed Unni. "Now somebody eats them," she said. "Like everybody else."
She set the plant back on the water, and Unni pushed off for school.
story.epiphany: For the parent: the ferns were not spreading because they were stronger plants. They were spreading because the insects who eat them had been left behind in Brazil. Ammu's clue was that every local plant had bite marks and the newcomer had none. This is one of the main explanations for invasive species. It is also why scientists sometimes bring a carefully tested natural enemy from the invader's homeland.
ask: Raking out forty lorry-loads did not clear the canal. Why not?
What did the holes in the lily and taro leaves tell Ammu?
The tea shop man said the payal were strong. What was a better explanation?
Why were the weevils kept in cages with rice and banana before anyone released them?
At the end, some payal still floated at the edges, with holes in them. Is that a failure? Why?

games.title: Could She Cross? An island card game
games.context: This is a card game about reaching an island. A new island lies 100 kilometres out to sea. Each card names a living being. You say whether they could get there without people, and how.

printables.title: 20 traveller cards to cut out (the answer is on the back)

items.b: Yes: floats. The thick husk is full of air. A coconut can float in the sea for many weeks and still sprout on a beach.
Yes: flies. Bats are the only native land mammals on many far islands.
Almost never. Salt water draws the water out through a frog's thin skin. Far islands have very few frogs.
Yes: flies. A young spider lets out a silk thread, and the wind carries them. A spider was the first animal found on Krakatau after the volcano exploded.

items.f: A river fish, such as a rohu
items.b: No. A river fish lives in fresh water, and the salty sea is a barrier for them.
Yes: rides. Geckos and their hard-shelled eggs travel in floating logs. Geckos live on many far islands.
No. A tiger swims rivers and tidal channels well, but 100 kilometres of open sea is too far.
Yes: flies. A fern's spores are as fine as dust, and wind carries them for hundreds of kilometres.
Almost never. Yet more than 25 million years ago some monkeys crossed from Africa to South America, probably on a raft of plants.
Yes: floats. Her long seedlings drop into the water, float away and take root where they settle in mud.
Only with people. Rats reached most of the world's islands by riding on ships.
Yes: floats. The mother lets her eggs go in the sea, and the tiny young drift for weeks before they come ashore.
Sometimes: rides. A nest inside a floating log can cross. Ants live on most islands, though fewer kinds than on the mainland.
Yes: floats. A tortoise floats, and can live for months without food or fresh water. That is how tortoises reached far islands.
Sometimes: rides. In 1995 at least fifteen iguanas reached the island of Anguilla on uprooted trees, after about 320 kilometres at sea.
Yes: flies. Globe skimmers fly across the open sea between India and East Africa.
No. Elephants swim well and cross wide rivers and narrow channels, but not 100 kilometres of open sea.

items.f: A grass seed stuck in mud on a bird's foot
items.b: Yes: rides. Wading birds carry seeds in the mud on their feet and in their droppings.

items.f: An earth-digging frog, such as the purple frog
items.b: No. She lives underground and comes up for about two weeks a year. Her relatives crossed the sea only because the land itself moved.
Yes: rides. People reached Australia by sea at least 50,000 years ago, on rafts or boats.

rules: Shuffle the cards and put them in a pile, with the names facing up. The island is 100 kilometres from the nearest land.
On your turn, read the top card aloud. Say 'crosses' or 'stays'. If you say 'crosses', also say how: flies, floats or rides.
Turn the card over and read the back aloud.
Score 1 point for the right choice of 'crosses' or 'stays'. Score 1 more point if you also gave the right way of crossing.
A back that begins 'Almost never', 'Sometimes' or 'Only with people' counts as right for either choice, if you gave a reason.
Take turns until the pile is finished. The player with the most points wins. If you play alone, play the pile twice and try to beat your first score.

flow.kid: Cut out the cards and shuffle them. Put a saucer far away. That is the island.

flow.do: 1. Take turns to read a card aloud. 2. The player says 'crosses' or 'stays', and how. 3. Turn the card over and read the back. 4. Write down the points.
flow.say: Ask yourself two things about each traveller. Can salt water hurt them? And do they have a way to fly, float or ride?

ask.q: Why can a spider reach an island that a frog cannot?
good: A young spider is carried by the wind on a silk thread.
A frog has to cross the water, and salt water harms a frog's skin.

flow.parent: Some answers are surprises. Children often expect the big, strong animals to cross and the tiny ones to stay. It is usually the other way round.

flow.kid: Sort the cards into 'cross' and 'stay'. Who will live on the island? Who will be missing?

check.q: Which group is most likely to be missing from a far island?
check.why: Frogs are harmed by salt water, so very few reach far islands. Birds and bats fly there, and fern spores blow there on the wind. If you chose birds or bats, think about who can cross water without touching it.

games.title: Native, Introduced or Invasive? A sorting card game about India
games.context: This is a card game about plants and animals in India. Each card names one. You decide whether they are native to India, introduced by people without harm, or invasive.

printables.title: 18 species cards to cut out (the answer is on the back)

items.b: Native. Neem trees have grown in India and nearby lands since long before people planted them.
Introduced. Chilli came from the Americas about 500 years ago. The plants grow where people sow them and do not spread through forests.

items.f: Lantana, a shrub with small pink and yellow flowers
items.b: Invasive. Lantana came from tropical America as a garden plant about 200 years ago. The shrubs now cover the ground in many forests.

items.f: Indian peafowl, the peacock and peahen
items.b: Native. Peafowl have always lived wild in India.
Introduced. Potatoes came from the Andes mountains of South America. They grow only where farmers plant them.

items.f: Water hyacinth, a floating plant with pale purple flowers
items.b: Invasive. Water hyacinth came from South America for garden ponds. A mat can double in size in one to two weeks.
Native. Pepper vines grow wild in the forests of the Western Ghats.
Introduced. Tapioca came from South America. In Kerala it is a much-loved food, and the plants stay in fields.
Invasive. Parthenium came from tropical America, probably as seeds mixed in grain. The weeds cover roadsides and fields and cause skin rashes.
Native. The banyan is a fig tree of India, and is the national tree.
Introduced. Cashew trees came from Brazil with Portuguese sailors. They grow in orchards along the coasts.
Invasive. These snails came from East Africa and were brought to India in 1847. They eat a very wide range of garden and farm plants.
Native. The ancestors of India's tigers walked here from the rest of Asia, with no help from people.
Introduced. Marigolds came from Mexico. People grow them for garlands, and they do not take over wild land.

items.f: African payal, the floating fern salvinia
items.b: Invasive. Salvinia came from Brazil and once choked the canals of Kuttanad in Kerala. A weevil from Brazil now keeps the ferns in check.
Native to India. But in Australia, where people took them in the 1860s, mynas are invasive.

items.f: Chital, the spotted deer, in the Andaman Islands
items.b: Invasive there. Chital are native to mainland India. People took them to the Andamans, where they eat the forest's seedlings.

items.f: Seemai karuvelam, a thorny tree planted for firewood
items.b: Invasive. These trees came from the Americas and were planted in dry parts of India from 1877. They have spread over large areas of dry land.

INVASIVE: brought by people, spreads alone and does harm

One player reads the top card aloud.
Everyone chooses one slip in secret and puts it face down. Then all turn their slips over together.
Turn the card over and read the back. Each player with the right slip scores 1 point.
A player who can say where the species came from scores 1 more point.
Play all 18 cards. The player with the most points wins. If you play alone, sort the whole pile into three heaps first, then check each card.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 18 cards and shuffle them. 2. Each player writes NATIVE, INTRODUCED and INVASIVE on three slips. 3. Read the three meanings aloud once.
flow.say: Native means they got here without people. Introduced means people brought them. Invasive means they were brought, spread alone and do harm.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Write three slips: NATIVE, INTRODUCED and INVASIVE.
flow.context: This is the first step of Native, Introduced or Invasive? Here you make the cards and the answer slips.

flow.do: 1. Read the top card aloud. 2. Everyone puts one slip face down. 3. Turn the slips over together. 4. Turn the card over and score.
flow.say: Two questions will help you. Did people bring them? And do they spread alone and harm others?
flow.kid: Read the card. Put one slip face down. Turn it over. Check the back of the card.

ask.q: Chilli and lantana both came from the Americas. Why is only lantana called invasive?
good: Chilli plants grow only where people sow them.
Lantana spreads alone through forests and shades out the grass.

flow.parent: The myna and chital cards are there to show that the answer depends on the place. Let your child argue about them.
flow.context: This is the main part of Native, Introduced or Invasive? Here you sort each plant or animal.

flow.say: Count the cards from the Americas. Why did so many newcomers to India come from there, and only in the last 500 years?
flow.kid: Count the cards from the Americas. Why so many? Why only in the last 500 years?

check.q: Why did plants from the Americas reach India only in the last 500 years?
options: Ships began to cross the oceans
check.why: Wide oceans were a barrier for millions of years. Sailing ships began to cross between the Americas, Europe and India about 500 years ago, and they carried plants with them. Continents move far too slowly to matter in 500 years.
