experiments.title: The Separated Lines Test: do two families of copies stay alike if they never mix?
experiments.context: In this experiment a line is copied by eye, and then the copy is copied, ten times over. Two families of copies are kept apart. Two other families are mixed at every step. You measure how far apart each pair ends.
experiments.question: Two families of lines both start from the same 100 millimetre line. Each new line is copied from the line before. If the two families never see each other, will they stay the same length? What if they are mixed at every step?
experiments.predict: Guess before you draw. After ten copies, how many millimetres apart will the two separated families be? How far apart will the two mixed families be? Why do you think so? Write both guesses and your reasons.
experiments.fair_test: All four families start from a line exactly 100 millimetres long. The same person makes every copy, with the same pencil, after looking for the same 3 seconds. Nobody uses a ruler while copying, and nobody looks back at older lines. Every family gets ten copies. Only one thing differs. Families A and B never see each other. Families C and D are copied from both at once. One run can be a fluke, so the last step tells you how to check your result.

materials.item: sheets of plain paper, A4 or pages from a long notebook
pencil
ruler marked in millimetres
folded newspaper or a thin towel, wide enough to cover two sheets side by side
notebook page for the results table

schedule.what: Draw four starting lines. Copy two families apart and two families mixed, ten times each. Measure every line and compare the gaps.

experiments.record: Draw a table with seven columns and eleven rows, for generations 0 to 10. Write the length of every line in millimetres, and the two gaps for each generation. Then write three sentences: what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results (all lengths in millimetres)
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished table can look like. Your numbers will be different.

setup.art: Four sheets of paper labelled A, B, C and D, each with one straight pencil line near the top and a ruler lying beside it showing 100 millimetres.
setup.caption: 1. Label four sheets A, B, C and D. Rule a line 100 millimetres long at the top of each.

setup.art: A child looking at the lowest line on sheet A while a folded newspaper covers all the lines above it.
setup.caption: 2. Look at the newest line for 3 seconds. Keep the older lines covered.

setup.art: The folded newspaper slid down to cover every line on the sheet, and the child's pencil drawing a new line freehand just below the newspaper.
setup.caption: 3. Cover the line. Draw a line of the same length below, without a ruler.

setup.art: Sheets C and D side by side under one folded newspaper, with the newest line of each showing and a child looking from one to the other.
setup.caption: 4. For C and D, look at both newest lines together. Draw one new line on each, halfway between them in length.

setup.art: A ruler laid along a pencil line and a table of numbers being filled in beside the sheet.
setup.caption: 5. Measure every line in millimetres. Find the gap for each pair.

flow.do: 1. Label four sheets A, B, C and D. 2. With the ruler, draw a line exactly 100 millimetres long near the top of each sheet. 3. Write 0 beside each line. 4. Draw the results table on a notebook page.
flow.say: Each sheet is one family. The ruled line is the first parent. Every new line will be a child, copied by eye from the line just before.
flow.kid: Label four sheets A, B, C and D. Rule a 100 millimetre line on each. Write 0 beside it.
flow.parent: Hold the sheets the tall way, so that eleven lines fit one under another. Leave about 2 centimetres between lines.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Separated Lines Test. Here you draw the four starting lines.

flow.do: 1. Explain the two rules: A and B are copied apart, and C and D are copied together. 2. Ask for both guesses and the reasons. 3. Write them down.
flow.say: After ten copies, how far apart will families A and B be? How far apart will C and D be? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess the gap between A and B after ten copies. Guess the gap between C and D. Say why. Write it down.

good: I copy carefully, so they will stay the same.
Small mistakes might add up.
C and D keep seeing each other, so they will stay close.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guesses. Many children expect all four families to stay at 100 millimetres, because they mean to copy carefully.
flow.context: This step of the Separated Lines Test is for guessing. You guess before you copy any lines.

flow.do: 1. Take sheet A alone. 2. Look at the newest line for 3 seconds. 3. Cover all the lines with the newspaper. 4. Draw a line of the same length just below, with no ruler. 5. Number it. 6. Do this ten times. 7. Turn sheet A face down and do the same on sheet B.
flow.say: Copy only the newest line each time. Look for three seconds, cover it, then draw. Do not peep at the older lines.
flow.kid: Look at the newest line for 3 seconds. Cover it. Draw the same length below. Do this ten times. Then do sheet B.
flow.parent: Count 'one and two and three' aloud for the look. Before each new look, slide the newspaper so that only the newest line shows. Sheet A must be out of sight while sheet B is done.
flow.context: In this step of the Separated Lines Test you copy families A and B. They are kept apart and never see each other.

flow.do: 1. Put sheets C and D side by side. 2. Uncover the newest line on both and look for 3 seconds. 3. Cover both. 4. Draw one new line on C and one on D. 5. Make each about halfway in length between the two lines you saw. 6. Do this ten times.
flow.say: This time the two families mix. Each child line has two parents, one from each sheet. Draw a length halfway between the two.
flow.kid: Put C and D side by side. Look at both newest lines. Cover them. Draw a halfway line on each. Do this ten times.
flow.parent: 'Halfway' is judged by eye. If the two lines look the same, your child simply copies that length. One look serves for both new lines.
flow.context: In this step of the Separated Lines Test you copy families C and D. Every new line is copied from both families together.

flow.do: 1. Measure every line with the ruler, to the nearest millimetre. 2. Write the lengths in the table. 3. For each generation, subtract to find the gap between A and B. 4. Do the same for C and D.
flow.say: Now we use the ruler. Measure each line and write it down. Then find the gap for each pair in every row.
flow.kid: Measure every line in millimetres. Write the lengths. Find the gap between A and B. Find the gap between C and D.
flow.parent: The gap is the longer length minus the shorter one, so it is never a minus number.
flow.context: In this step of the Separated Lines Test you measure all the lines and find how far apart each pair of families is.

flow.do: 1. Compare the last row: which pair ended further apart? 2. Count the rows in which the A and B gap is the bigger one. 3. Ask your child what they thought, what they saw and why it happened. 4. Then read the note below together.
flow.say: Which pair ended further apart? In how many rows was the A and B gap bigger? Say what you thought, what you saw, and why you think it happened.
flow.kid: Which pair ended further apart? Say what you thought, what you saw and why it happened.

ask.q: You tried to copy every line exactly. So where did the difference between A and B come from?
good: Each copy had a small mistake.
The next copy was made from the mistaken line, so mistakes were passed on.
A and B made different mistakes and nothing brought them back together.

ask.q: Why did C and D stay close to each other?
good: Each new line was made from both families.
A mistake in one family was shared with the other at the next step.

check.q: What kept families C and D close to each other?
options: They were mixed at every step
check.why: C and D were mixed at every step, so any change in one was shared with the other. The care, the first line and the number of copies were the same for all four families. If you chose 'more carefully', look again at the fair test: the copier and the look time did not change.

flow.parent: In most runs A and B end 10 to 40 millimetres apart, and C and D end less than 10 millimetres apart. All four families may also shrink or grow together, because most people copy a little short or a little long. That is fine: the test is about the gap inside each pair. About one run in five, A and B end close by chance, the way two people taking random steps can end up side by side. Then look at how many rows had the bigger gap between A and B, or run a third separated family on a new sheet. The reason: every copy has a small mistake, and the next copy is made from the mistaken line. In a separated family the mistakes pile up, and no other family corrects them. This is a model of living beings. Parents copy their DNA for their young, and each copy has a few small mistakes. In one large group, young have parents from all over the group, so changes are shared. A barrier such as a sea stops the sharing. The model leaves two things out. In real life many copies are made at once and chance decides which are kept. Natural selection also pushes each group to suit its own place.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Separated Lines Test. You compare the separated families with the mixed families and explain the difference.

experiments.title: The Far Island Test: do fewer travellers reach a far island than a near one?
experiments.context: In this experiment rice grains stand for seeds and small animals blown or washed out to sea. You pour rice onto an upturned bowl so that the grains scatter. You count how many land in bowls placed near, further and furthest away.
experiments.question: Grains scatter from one spot in all directions. Three bowls of the same size stand at one, two and three steps of distance. How many grains land in each? Does a bowl twice as far away catch half as many? Does a wide plate catch more than a small bowl at the same distance?
experiments.predict: Guess before you pour. If the near bowl catches 30 grains, how many will the bowl twice as far away catch: 30, 15, or fewer than 15? Will a wide plate catch more than a small bowl at the same distance? Why do you think so? Write your guesses and reasons.
experiments.fair_test: Use the same spoon of rice, poured from the same height onto the same spot, for every pour. The three island bowls are the same size, and each has a cloth inside so that grains do not bounce out. Only the distance changes. In the second part, only the size of the island changes. Pour three times and add the counts, because grains bounce differently each time.

materials.item: raw rice
steel katoris (small bowls) of the same size: one to turn upside down and three to be islands
steel plate about 25 centimetres wide
clean bedsheet to spread on the floor
handkerchiefs or pieces of cloth, to line the island bowls and the plate
ruler or measuring tape
tablespoon

schedule.what: Scatter rice from an upturned bowl. Count the grains caught at three distances, then on a small and a large island.

experiments.record: Fill in the table for the three distances. Add two more rows for the small bowl and the wide plate at the same distance. Then write three sentences: what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: grains caught in three pours
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Your numbers will be different.

setup.art: A bedsheet spread on a floor with one steel bowl turned upside down in the middle, and three small steel bowls lined with cloth standing at different distances in three different directions.
setup.caption: 1. Turn one bowl upside down in the middle of the sheet. Stand three lined bowls at 10, 20 and 30 centimetres.

setup.art: A child standing over the upturned bowl and pouring a spoonful of rice onto its top from waist height, with grains bouncing outward.
setup.caption: 2. Pour one spoon of rice slowly onto the top of the upturned bowl.

setup.art: A child tipping the grains from one small bowl onto a dark cloth and counting them with a fingertip.
setup.caption: 3. Count the grains in each island bowl. Pour three times in all.

flow.do: 1. Spread the bedsheet on the floor. 2. Turn one katori upside down in the middle. 3. Line three katoris with cloth. 4. Pour one trial spoon of rice onto the upturned katori from waist height. 5. See how far most grains go.
flow.say: The upturned bowl is the mainland. The grains are seeds and tiny animals swept out to sea. Let's see how far they scatter.
flow.kid: Spread the sheet. Turn one bowl upside down. Pour one spoon of rice on top. See how far the grains go.
flow.parent: Grains usually land within 30 centimetres on a sheet. Put the near bowl where plenty of grains fell, often about 10 centimetres from the edge of the upturned bowl. Put the other two at twice and three times that distance, each in a different direction. Pick up the trial rice first.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Far Island Test. Here you set up the mainland and three island bowls on a sheet.

flow.do: 1. Show the three island bowls. 2. Ask how many grains the further bowls will catch, if the near bowl catches 30. 3. Ask whether a wide plate will catch more. 4. Write the guesses and reasons.
flow.say: If the near island catches 30 grains, how many will the one twice as far catch? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess how many grains each bowl will catch. Say why. Write it down.

good: Fewer grains bounce that far.
Twice as far might mean half as many.
Far away, the grains are spread over more floor.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Most children guess half as many at twice the distance.
flow.context: This step of the Far Island Test is for guessing. You guess before you pour the rice.

flow.do: 1. Pour one level tablespoon of rice slowly onto the top of the upturned katori. 2. Count the grains in each island bowl and write them down. 3. Empty the bowls. 4. Do this three times. 5. Add up each bowl's three counts.
flow.say: Pour from the same height each time. Then count each island's grains. We pour three times, because the grains bounce differently each time.
flow.kid: Pour one spoon of rice on the bowl. Count the grains on each island. Do it three times. Add them up.
flow.parent: If the furthest bowl catches nothing in three pours, that is a real result. Write 0. If even the near bowl catches fewer than 5, move all three bowls closer and start again.
flow.context: In this step of the Far Island Test you scatter the rice and count the grains that reach each island.

flow.do: 1. Take away the near and furthest bowls. 2. Put the cloth-lined plate at the middle distance, in a new direction. 3. Pour three spoons, one at a time. 4. Count the grains on the plate and in the middle bowl.
flow.say: Now a small island and a large island are at the same distance. Which will catch more travellers? Let's count.
flow.kid: Put the plate at the middle distance. Pour three spoons. Count the grains on the plate and in the bowl.
flow.context: In this step of the Far Island Test you compare a small island with a large island at the same distance.

flow.do: 1. Look at the totals together. 2. Ask your child what they thought, what they saw and why it happened. 3. Read the note below together. 4. Wash the rice and cook it.
flow.say: Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why you think it happened. Was twice as far half as many?
flow.kid: Say what you thought, what you saw and why it happened. Was twice as far half as many?

ask.q: Why did the far bowl catch far fewer than half as many grains?
good: Fewer grains travel that far.
The grains that do go far are spread round a much bigger circle.
The bowl covers a smaller share of that circle.

ask.q: What does this say about an island far out at sea?
good: Very few living beings reach it.
It will have fewer kinds than a near island.

check.q: Two islands are the same size. One is near the mainland and one is far. Which is likely to have more kinds of living beings?
check.why: More travellers reach the near island, so more kinds settle there. Size was the same, so only distance differed. If you chose 'both the same', look at your own counts for the near and far bowls.

flow.parent: In most homes the near bowl catches several times as many grains as the middle bowl, and the furthest catches almost none. Two things work together. Few grains bounce far. And those that do are spread round a wider ring of floor, so one bowl covers a smaller share of the ring. The wide plate catches several times as many as the small bowl beside it, because it covers more floor. Real islands follow the same two rules. In 1967 Robert MacArthur and Edward Wilson wrote that near islands and large islands get more arrivals. The model leaves out what happens after landing. On a real island a traveller must also find food and a mate.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Far Island Test. You compare the near, further and furthest islands and explain the counts.

activities.title: Who Lives Where? Eight animals on a world map
activities.context: In this activity you place eight animals on a simple world map, each on the land where they live wild. Then you look for anything odd in the pattern.

materials.item: sheet of plain paper
pencil
school atlas, a globe or a world map on a phone, to copy from
small slips of paper

activities.record: Keep the map. Under it write one thing you noticed and one question you want answered.

setup.art: A child's rough pencil map of the world on one sheet of paper, with seven blobs for the continents labelled by name.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a rough world map: seven blobs for the continents, each with a name.

setup.art: Eight small paper slips with animal names being placed on the hand-drawn map, a penguin slip at the bottom and a polar bear slip at the top.
setup.caption: 2. Write eight animal names on slips. Put each where the animal lives wild.

setup.art: A child pointing at the empty Arctic on the map and then at the penguin slip in the far south, looking puzzled.
setup.caption: 3. Look for places that would suit an animal who is not there.

flow.do: 1. Look at a world map together. 2. Your child draws seven rough blobs for the continents and names them. 3. Mark the North Pole and the South Pole. 4. Mark Madagascar and India.
flow.say: The shapes can be rough. We only need to know which land is which, and where the two poles are.
flow.kid: Draw seven blobs for the continents. Name them. Mark the two poles, Madagascar and India.
flow.parent: The seven continents are Asia, Africa, Europe, North America, South America, Australia and Antarctica. Madagascar is the large island beside southern Africa.
flow.context: This is the first step of Who Lives Where? Here you draw a rough map of the world.

flow.do: 1. Write these names on eight slips: penguin, polar bear, kangaroo, tiger, lemur, hummingbird, giraffe, camel. 2. Your child puts each slip where they think that animal lives wild. 3. Check with the list in the note below.
flow.say: Put each animal where you think they live in the wild, with no zoo and no help from people.
flow.kid: Write eight animal names on slips. Put each where the animal lives wild. Check with a grown-up.
flow.parent: Penguins: Antarctica and other southern coasts. Polar bears: the Arctic, around the North Pole. Kangaroos: Australia and New Guinea. Tigers: Asia. Lemurs: Madagascar only. Hummingbirds: North and South America only. Giraffes: Africa. Camels: Asia and Africa. Camels also live wild in Australia now, but people took them there.
flow.context: In this step of Who Lives Where? you place eight animals on your map.

flow.do: 1. Ask what your child notices about the map. 2. Ask what they wonder. 3. Ask about the two cold ends of the Earth. 4. Write down one question to answer later.
flow.say: What do you notice? What do you wonder? Both poles are icy. Why do penguins live at only one, and polar bears at only the other?
flow.kid: What do you notice? Both poles are icy. Why are penguins at only one? Write one question.

ask.q: India has forests full of flowers. Why might there be no hummingbirds in India?
good: Maybe they could never get here.
The sea is in the way.
Other birds, like sunbirds, do that job here.

flow.think: Is there any place that would suit you, where no people have ever lived?
flow.parent: Do not explain yet. Good answers begin with 'maybe they could not get there'. The rest of the unit answers the question.
flow.context: This is the last step of Who Lives Where? Here you look for patterns in the map and ask your own question.

activities.title: The Gondwana Jigsaw: do the fossils line up?
activities.context: In this activity you trace the southern continents, cut them out and fit them together into Gondwana. Then you check whether fossil finds on separate continents meet when the pieces are joined.

materials.item: school atlas, or a world map on a phone or a calendar
thin paper to trace through, such as butter paper or a page from a thin notebook
pencil, two colour pencils and scissors
sheet of plain paper and glue or tape

activities.safety: Scissors are sharp. A grown-up helps a younger child to cut.
activities.record: Glue the pieces in their Gondwana positions on one half of the sheet. On the other half draw India where it is today, with an arrow for the journey. Write one sentence about the fossils.

setup.art: Thin paper laid over a world map in an atlas, with a child tracing the outline of Africa in pencil.
setup.caption: 1. Trace South America, Africa, Madagascar, India, Australia and Antarctica.

setup.art: Six cut-out paper continents, each with coloured dots: green on all six and orange on India, southern Africa and Antarctica.
setup.caption: 2. Cut them out. Colour the fossil places from the list.

setup.art: The cut-out continents pushed together into one large land, with the green and orange patches joined into single areas, and India being slid away northward by a finger.
setup.caption: 3. Fit the pieces together. Then slide India north, away from Madagascar.

flow.do: 1. Lay thin paper over the world map. 2. Trace South America, Africa, Madagascar, India, Australia and Antarctica. 3. Write each name inside. 4. Cut the six pieces out.
flow.say: We need six pieces of land. Trace round each one, write the name inside, and cut each out.
flow.kid: Trace six lands from the map. Write each name inside. Cut them out.
flow.parent: Rough edges are fine. On a flat map Antarctica is stretched along the bottom, so draw it as a rough oval about the size of Australia. If you have a globe, copy the shapes from it by eye.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Gondwana Jigsaw. Here you trace and cut out six pieces of land.

flow.do: 1. With green, shade part of all six pieces: the Glossopteris plant grew on every one. 2. With orange, mark southern Africa, India and Antarctica: Lystrosaurus fossils lie there. 3. Ask how one land animal could be on three lands.
flow.say: Lystrosaurus was a land animal about as long as a goat. Her fossils lie in Africa, India and Antarctica. How could that be?
flow.kid: Shade all six pieces green for one fossil plant. Mark Africa, India and Antarctica orange for one fossil animal.

ask.q: How could the same land animal have lived on three lands with oceans between them?
good: Maybe she swam, but the oceans are thousands of kilometres wide.
Maybe there were bridges of land.
Maybe the lands were once joined.

flow.parent: Take every idea seriously. A sunken land bridge was the answer most geologists gave until the 1960s. Lystrosaurus was a plant-eater about 1 metre long, who lived about 250 million years ago.
flow.context: In this step of the Gondwana Jigsaw you mark where two kinds of fossils are found.

flow.do: 1. Fit South America against the west side of Africa. 2. Put Madagascar and India against the east side of Africa. 3. Put Antarctica below them and Australia beside Antarctica. 4. Look at the coloured patches.
flow.say: Push the pieces together like a jigsaw. Now look at the orange marks. What has happened to them?
flow.kid: Fit the six pieces into one big land. Look at the orange marks. What do you see?

check.q: When the pieces are joined, the fossil places meet. What does this suggest?
options: The same animal arose three times
The fossils were carried by people
check.why: On the joined land, the fossil places lie side by side, so the animal lived in one area. That fits the idea that the lands were joined. A land animal could not swim thousands of kilometres of ocean, and the same animal arising three times is far less likely.

flow.parent: The fit is rough, because paper continents are flat and the real edges lie under shallow sea. India's west coast goes against Madagascar's east coast. Antarctica sits against India's east coast and the south of Africa.
flow.context: In this step of the Gondwana Jigsaw you join the six pieces and see whether the fossil places meet.

flow.do: 1. Slide India slowly north, leaving Madagascar behind. 2. Stop when India would meet Asia. 3. Glue the pieces down. 4. Draw an arrow for India's journey.
flow.say: India left Madagascar roughly 90 million years ago and met Asia about 50 million years ago. Suppose frogs lived on both pieces. What happened to them?
flow.kid: Slide India north, away from Madagascar. Glue the pieces down. Draw an arrow for India's journey.

ask.q: Frogs lived on the land before it split. What happened to the two groups afterwards?
good: They could not meet any more.
They changed separately and became different kinds.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Gondwana Jigsaw. Here you move India north and think about the animals on board.

activities.title: Land Bridge in a Tray: which island could animals walk to?
activities.context: In this activity you build a mainland and two islands from dough in a tray of water. One channel is shallow and one is deep. You lower the water, as an ice age does, and see which island joins the mainland.

materials.item: deep tray, a baking dish or a wide steel basin
stiff atta dough or modelling clay, about two handfuls
water and a small cup for taking water out
ruler

activities.record: Draw the tray from the side twice: with high water and with low water. Label the mainland, the two islands, the shallow channel and the deep channel.

setup.art: A baking dish with a slab of dough along one side as the mainland, two lumps of dough as islands, a thin layer of dough on the floor of the dish between the mainland and the first island, and bare dish floor before the second island.
setup.caption: 1. Build a mainland and two islands. Make the first channel shallow and the second one deep.

setup.art: The same dish filled with water so that only the tops of the mainland and the two islands show.
setup.caption: 2. Pour in water until both channels are covered.

setup.art: A child scooping water out with a cup, and the shallow channel now showing as a strip of wet dough joining the mainland to the first island.
setup.caption: 3. Take water out, a cup at a time. Watch which island joins the mainland.

flow.do: 1. Press a slab of dough 4 centimetres high along one side of the tray. 2. Make two island lumps 4 centimetres high. 3. Between the mainland and island 1, lay dough 3 centimetres deep. 4. Leave the tray floor bare between island 1 and island 2.
flow.say: This is a mainland and two islands. The sea floor between the first two is high. Beyond the second it drops away.
flow.kid: Build a mainland and two islands. Make the first sea floor high. Leave the second sea floor low.
flow.parent: The dough between the mainland and island 1 is a shallow sea floor, 1 centimetre lower than the land. The bare tray between the islands is a deep channel.
flow.context: This is the first step of Land Bridge in a Tray. Here you build the land and the sea floor from dough.

flow.do: 1. Pour in water until it is about 3 and a half centimetres deep. 2. Ask which island an animal could walk to if the sea went down. 3. Ask why. 4. Take water out, one cup at a time.
flow.say: In an ice age, water is locked up as ice on the land, so the sea falls. Which island will join the mainland first? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Pour in water. Guess which island will join the mainland. Say why. Take water out slowly.

good: The sea floor is higher between the mainland and island 1.
The shallow part will dry first.

flow.context: In this step of Land Bridge in a Tray you fill the sea and then lower it, as an ice age does.

flow.do: 1. Stop when the shallow channel is dry land. 2. Walk two fingers from the mainland to island 1. 3. Try to walk to island 2. 4. Pour the water back and watch the bridge go under.
flow.say: Island 1 is joined now, and island 2 is still cut off. Which real islands are like island 1, and which like island 2?
flow.kid: Walk your fingers to island 1. Can they reach island 2? Pour the water back.

check.q: In the last ice age the sea fell about 120 metres. Which sea became dry land?
check.why: Only sea floor less than about 120 metres deep was uncovered. The sea between India and Sri Lanka is at most about 35 metres deep, so it became dry land. Deep channels stayed sea, however narrow they were.

flow.parent: Sri Lanka is like island 1: the sea between Sri Lanka and India is very shallow, and animals walked across until about 7,000 years ago. Lombok in Indonesia is like island 2: a deep channel kept it apart from Bali.
flow.context: This is the last step of Land Bridge in a Tray. Here you see that a shallow sea makes a bridge and a deep sea does not.

activities.title: Your Nail and India: how slow is a moving continent?
activities.context: In this two-week activity you measure how fast your thumbnail grows. Then you compare your nail with the speed of the land you live on. The Indian plate moves about 5 centimetres a year.

materials.item: nail polish, or a permanent marker
ruler marked in millimetres
notebook

schedule.what: Paint a thin line across the base of one thumbnail, touching the skin. Write the date.
Measure the bare gap between the skin and the line. Work out the growth in a year, and compare it with India's speed.

activities.record: Write the date, the gap in millimetres after 14 days, and your sum for one year. Then write which moves faster: your nail or India.

setup.art: A close view of a child's thumb with a thin line of nail polish painted across the nail right where it meets the skin.
setup.caption: 1. Paint a thin line across the base of your thumbnail, touching the skin.

setup.art: The same thumb two weeks later with a thin bare gap between the skin and the painted line, and a ruler held beside the nail.
setup.caption: 2. After 14 days, measure the bare gap that has grown in below the line.

flow.do: 1. Paint a thin line across the base of one thumbnail, touching the skin. 2. Let it dry. 3. Ask how far the nail will grow in 14 days, and why. 4. Write the date and the guess.
flow.say: Your nail grows from under the skin and pushes this line forward. How many millimetres will it move in two weeks? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Paint a thin line at the base of your thumbnail. Guess how far it will move in 14 days. Write the date.
flow.parent: If the line wears off in the bath, paint it again in the same place on the nail. A scratch made gently with a nail file also works as a mark.
flow.context: This is the first step of Your Nail and India. Here you mark your thumbnail so that you can measure how fast it grows.

flow.do: 1. Measure the bare gap between the skin and the line. 2. Multiply by 26 to get the growth in a year. 3. Change it to centimetres. 4. Compare it with 5 centimetres, the Indian plate's yearly movement.
flow.say: There are 26 two-week stretches in a year, so multiply by 26. Is your nail faster or slower than India?
flow.kid: Measure the bare gap in millimetres. Multiply by 26. Is your nail faster or slower than India?
flow.wait: Do this 14 days after painting the line

ask.q: India moves about as fast as a nail grows. How could something so slow cross an ocean?
good: It had a very long time.
A few centimetres a year for millions of years adds up to thousands of kilometres.

flow.parent: Most thumbnails grow about 1 and a half millimetres in two weeks. That is about 4 centimetres a year, a little slower than the Indian plate. The gap is small, so measure in good light. A result of 1 or 2 millimetres is equally fine.
flow.context: This is the last step of Your Nail and India. Here you measure your nail's growth and compare it with the speed of the Indian plate.

activities.title: Count the Bites: is a newcomer plant eaten less? (if you have a street, a garden or a park nearby)
activities.context: In this outdoor activity you look at twenty leaves of a plant native to India and twenty leaves of a plant introduced from another continent. You count how many leaves have holes or chewed edges.

materials.item: notebook and pencil
a native plant and an introduced plant growing near each other (see the list in step 1)

activities.safety: Look at the leaves on the plant without picking them. Do not touch parthenium, the weed with tiny white flowers, because these plants give many people a rash. Wash your hands afterwards.
activities.record: Write the two plant names and two numbers: leaves with bites out of 20, for each plant. Add one sentence on what you found and one on why your result could be wrong.

setup.art: A child with a notebook looking closely at the leaves of a roadside tree, with a flowering lantana bush a few steps away.
setup.caption: 1. Find a native plant and an introduced plant growing near each other.

setup.art: A close view of a branch with some leaves whole and some with holes and chewed edges, and a finger pointing at each leaf in turn.
setup.caption: 2. Look at 20 leaves on each plant, one after another. Count those with holes or chewed edges.

flow.do: 1. Find one native plant: neem, pongam, peepal, banyan, jamun or curry leaf. 2. Find one introduced plant nearby: lantana, bougainvillea, gulmohar, rain tree or eucalyptus. 3. Ask which will have more bitten leaves, and why.
flow.say: One of these plants has lived in India for a very long time. The other was brought from far away. Which will have more bitten leaves? Why?
flow.kid: Find a native plant and an introduced plant. Guess which has more bitten leaves. Say why.
flow.parent: Choose two plants of about the same height, both in sun or both in shade. A phone app for naming plants can help. If you cannot find a pair, compare any two kinds and still count.
flow.context: This is the first step of Count the Bites. Here you choose two plants and make a guess.

flow.do: 1. On the first plant, choose a branch without looking closely. 2. Look at 20 leaves in a row along it. 3. Count the leaves with a hole, a chewed edge or a tunnel. 4. Do the same on the second plant.
flow.say: Take twenty leaves in a row, not the ones you like. Count each leaf that somebody has eaten from.
flow.kid: Look at 20 leaves in a row. Count the ones with holes or chewed edges. Do both plants.
flow.parent: Taking leaves in a row stops the eye from picking out the damaged ones. Count a leaf once, however many holes it has.
flow.context: In this step of Count the Bites you count the bitten leaves on each plant.

flow.do: 1. Compare the two numbers. 2. Ask what your child thought, what they saw and why it might be so. 3. Ask what else could explain the result.
flow.say: Say what you thought, what you saw, and why it might be so. What else could explain it, apart from where the plant came from?
flow.kid: Compare your two numbers. Say what you thought and what you saw. What else could explain it?

ask.q: What else, apart from the plant's homeland, could make one plant less bitten?
good: Tougher or hairier leaves.
Poison in the leaves.
Younger leaves.
One plant may have been sprayed.

flow.parent: Often the introduced plant has fewer bitten leaves, because the insects who feed on that plant live on another continent. But your result may go the other way, and one pair of plants proves little. Scientists who compared many pairs found the pattern in some studies and not in others. Tell your child that this is still argued about.
flow.context: This is the last step of Count the Bites. Here you compare the two plants and think about what the result can and cannot show.

projects.title: A Newcomer's File: one introduced plant or animal near your home
projects.context: In this three-day project you choose one plant or animal who was brought to India by people. You find out where they came from, how they travelled, what they changed here, and what people are doing about it.

materials.item: sheets of plain paper, folded into a small file
school atlas or a world map on a phone
phone or library book, for looking things up with a grown-up
pencils and colour pencils

schedule.what: Choose your newcomer. Find their homeland and mark the journey to India on a map. Find out who brought them, when and why.
Find out what they changed in India: who lost, who gained, and who uses them now.
Write what is being done, and what you would do. Present the file.

projects.record: A three-page file. Page 1: a drawing of the newcomer and a map of the journey. Page 2: a table with two columns, 'who lost' and 'who gained'. Page 3: what is being done, and your own plan with one reason.

setup.art: A child drawing a lantana sprig on the first page of a paper file, with an atlas open at a world map and an arrow pencilled from South America to India.
setup.caption: 1. Choose one newcomer. Draw them, and map the journey to India.

setup.art: A page with a two-column table headed 'who lost' and 'who gained', with small drawings of a deer, a butterfly and a basket maker.
setup.caption: 2. Make a table of who lost and who gained.

setup.art: A child holding up a finished three-page file and explaining it to two grown-ups.
setup.caption: 3. Write what you would do, and present your file.

flow.do: 1. Choose one: lantana, water hyacinth, parthenium, the giant African snail, seemai karuvelam, gulmohar, eucalyptus, or the chilli plant. 2. Find the homeland. 3. Draw the journey to India on a map. 4. Find out who brought them, when and why.
flow.say: Choose a newcomer you can see near home, if you can. Where is their homeland? How did they cross the sea, and who wanted them here?
flow.kid: Choose one newcomer. Find their homeland. Draw the journey on a map. Find who brought them and why.
flow.parent: Some answers are not known for certain, and it is good to write 'nobody is sure'. A harmless newcomer such as chilli or gulmohar is as good a choice as an invasive one.
flow.context: This is day 1 of A Newcomer's File. Here you choose a plant or animal and trace their journey to India.

flow.do: 1. Find out what changed after the newcomer arrived. 2. List who lost: plants, animals or people. 3. List who gained. 4. Find one use people have made of the newcomer.
flow.say: Every newcomer changes something. Who has less because of them? Who has more? Has anybody found a use for them?
flow.kid: Find what changed. List who lost and who gained. Find one use people made.

ask.q: Can the same newcomer be bad for one living being and good for another?
good: Yes. Lantana shades out grass that deer eat, but some birds eat the berries.
It depends on who you ask.

flow.context: This is day 2 of A Newcomer's File. Here you find out who lost and who gained from the newcomer.

flow.do: 1. Find out what is being done: pulling out, a natural enemy, a law, or nothing. 2. Your child writes their own plan and one reason. 3. Your child presents the file to the family.
flow.say: What are people doing about this newcomer? What would you do, and why? What might go wrong with your plan?
flow.kid: Find what people are doing. Write your own plan and a reason. Show your file to the family.
flow.parent: A good plan says what it costs, who it helps and what might go wrong. 'Leave them alone' is a fair plan if your child gives a reason.
flow.context: This is day 3 of A Newcomer's File. Here you decide what you would do, and present your file.

challenges.title: Clear the Tank: beat a water weed that doubles
challenges.context: This is a planning challenge on paper. A floating weed covers one square of a tank drawn as 64 squares. Every round the weed doubles. You must find a plan that clears the tank with the fewest squares of work.
challenges.problem: A village tank is drawn as a grid of 64 squares. A water weed covers 1 square. Each round stands for two weeks, and in each round the weed doubles. After the doubling, your team may clear some squares. Find a plan that clears the whole tank, and uses as little work as possible.
constraints: In every round the weed doubles first. Then you clear.
In the first two parts your team can clear at most 3 squares in a round.
If the weed covers all 64 squares, the tank is lost.
In your own plan you have 30 squares of clearing work in total, to spend in any rounds you choose.
materials: a sheet of paper and a ruler, to draw a grid of 8 squares by 8 squares
64 dry beans, such as rajma or chana, or 64 small bits of paper
a pencil and a notebook page for the count in each round
general: Clear 3 squares in every round, starting in round 1.
Wait until the weed is easy to see, then clear as hard as you can.
Clear only the squares near the bank, where people fetch water.
creative: Pay one person to walk round the tank every week, so that the first plant is seen at once.
Stretch a floating rope across the tank, so that the weed is held in one corner while you clear.
Release a tested natural enemy that slows the doubling, and clear by hand as well.
challenges.your_turn: Now make your own plan. You have 30 squares of clearing work in total. The weed already covers 4 squares when you first notice. In which rounds will you spend your work? Play it with the beans. Did you clear the tank? What would you tell a village that has just found its first water hyacinth?

setup.art: A hand-drawn grid of 8 by 8 squares on paper with one bean on one square, and a small heap of beans beside the paper.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a tank of 64 squares. Put 1 bean on the grid for the weed.

setup.art: The same grid with 8 beans on it and a child adding 8 more, while a notebook beside it lists 1, 2, 4, 8, 16.
setup.caption: 2. Each round, double the beans. Then take away the squares you clear.

flow.do: 1. Draw the grid of 64 squares. 2. Put 1 bean on the grid. 3. Ask how many rounds it will take to fill the tank if nobody clears, and why. 4. Double the beans each round and write the count.
flow.say: The weed doubles every round. How many rounds until the tank is full? Why do you think so? Let's play it with no clearing.
flow.kid: Draw 64 squares. Put on 1 bean. Guess how many rounds fill the tank. Double the beans each round.

ask.q: The tank is full after round 6. In which round was it half full?
good: Round 5, only one round earlier.
A half-full tank is one doubling away from full.

flow.parent: The counts are 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 and 64. The tank is full after 6 rounds, which stands for 12 weeks. Many children guess 30 rounds or more.
flow.context: This is the first step of Clear the Tank. Here you watch a weed that doubles fill the tank when nobody clears.

flow.do: 1. Start again with 1 bean. 2. Each round, double the beans and then remove 3. 3. Play again, but begin clearing only when there are 2 beans. 4. Play again from 3 beans, and then from 4 beans.
flow.say: Your team clears 3 squares a round. Does it matter when you start? Try starting at 1, 2, 3 and 4 beans.
flow.kid: Double the beans, then take away 3. Try starting at 1, 2, 3 and 4 beans. What happens each time?

ask.q: Why can 3 squares of clearing never beat 4 squares of weed?
good: 4 doubles to 8, and 8 take away 3 is 5, which is more than before.
The weed adds more each round than the team can remove.

check.q: A team clears 3 squares each round, after the weed doubles. From which start can they clear the tank?
check.why: From 2 squares: 2 doubles to 4, less 3 leaves 1. Then 1 doubles to 2, and 3 clears it. From 3 squares the weed returns to 3 every round, for ever. From 4 it grows. The team wins only while the weed is smaller than what they can clear.

flow.parent: From 1 bean the tank is clear in one round. From 2 beans it takes two rounds. From 3 beans the count stays at 3 for ever. From 4 beans the weed wins. The rule: you win only if you can clear more than is there now.
flow.context: In this step of Clear the Tank you test whether a team that clears 3 squares a round can win from different starts.

flow.do: 1. Read the task under 'Your turn' together. 2. Your child plans how to spend 30 squares of work, starting from 4 beans. 3. Play the plan with the beans. 4. Compare an early plan with a late plan.
flow.say: You have 30 squares of work, and the weed covers 4 squares. When will you spend the work? Why? Play it and see.
flow.kid: You have 30 squares of work. The weed covers 4. Plan when to clear. Play your plan.
flow.parent: Spending 8 at once wins: 4 doubles to 8, and 8 are cleared. Waiting two rounds means 16 double to 32, which is more than 30. The same work that wins early loses late. Real water hyacinth mats can double in one to two weeks.
flow.context: This is the last step of Clear the Tank. Here you make your own plan with a fixed amount of work.

challenges.title: The Stowaway Check: find every seed before the ship unloads
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. A grown-up hides mustard seeds in five kinds of cargo. You are the inspector at an island's harbour. You design a way to find every seed in five minutes, using kitchen tools.
challenges.problem: A ship is arriving at an island that has no weeds from outside. Seeds may be hidden in the cargo. A grown-up hides 15 mustard seeds: 3 in each of five kinds of cargo. Design a check for each kind of cargo. Find as many seeds as you can in 5 minutes, without spoiling the cargo.
constraints: You have 5 minutes for the whole ship.
The cargo must still be usable afterwards. The dal must still be fit to cook.
You may use any kitchen tool, but you must choose your tools before the clock starts.
You may refuse one kind of cargo and send it back, but that costs 2 points.
materials: 15 mustard seeds, or ragi or sesame seeds
a cup of chana dal, or any split dal
a chappal or shoe with a little wet atta paste pressed on the sole
a small bowl of dry soil or sand
kitchen tools to choose from: a plate, a strainer, a colander, a clean cloth, a spoon, a sheet of newspaper, an old toothbrush
general: Spread the dal on a plate and pick the seeds out by eye.
Shake the towel over a sheet of newspaper.
Look at the sole of the chappal and pick the seeds off.
creative: Tilt a plate of split dal a little and tap it. Round seeds roll down, and flat dal stays.
Pour the tumbler of water through a clean cloth, as ports can filter the water that ships carry for balance.
Brush the sole over white paper with an old toothbrush, as some countries make travellers clean their shoes.
Refuse the soil. Many countries do not let travellers bring in any soil, because seeds and tiny animals in it are too hard to find.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own check and run it against the clock. Score 1 point for each seed found. Take off 2 points if you refused a cargo, and 2 points for each cargo you spoiled. Which cargo was hardest? What rule would you make for a real island harbour?

setup.art: Five things in a row on a table: a cup of dal, a chappal with pale paste on its sole, a folded hand towel, a tumbler of water and a small bowl of soil, with a few tiny dark seeds shown beside them.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up hides 3 seeds in each of five kinds of cargo.

setup.art: A child tilting a steel plate of split dal so that tiny round seeds roll to the low edge, with a strainer, a cloth and a toothbrush laid out nearby and a phone timer running.
setup.caption: 2. Choose your tools. Find as many seeds as you can in 5 minutes.

flow.do: 1. Send your child out of the room. 2. Stir 3 seeds into the dal and 3 into the soil. 3. Press 3 into the paste on the sole. 4. Fold 3 into the towel. 5. Drop 3 into the water.
flow.say: I am loading the ship. Come back when I call. Then you will be the harbour inspector for an island.
flow.kid: Wait outside while the seeds are hidden. Then you are the harbour inspector.
flow.parent: If your child works alone, they hide the seeds with their eyes half closed and mix well. Seeds in water mostly sink within a minute.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Stowaway Check. Here a grown-up hides seeds in five kinds of cargo.

flow.do: 1. Show the five kinds of cargo and the tools. 2. Your child plans a check for each cargo and says why it should work. 3. Your child lays out the chosen tools.
flow.say: Seeds could be in any of these. How will you check each one quickly? Why should your way work? Choose your tools now.
flow.kid: Look at the five kinds of cargo. Plan a check for each. Say why it should work. Choose your tools.

ask.q: Which cargo do you expect to be hardest, and why?
good: The soil, because the seeds look like grains of soil.
The dal, because there is so much of it.

flow.context: In this step of the Stowaway Check you design a way to check each kind of cargo.

flow.do: 1. Start a 5 minute timer. 2. Your child runs the checks. 3. Count the seeds found and work out the score. 4. Search slowly for the seeds that were missed. 5. Talk about the rule your child would make for a real harbour.
flow.say: Go! When the timer rings, we count. Then we look for the ones that got past you, and ask how they did it.
flow.kid: Start the timer. Run your checks. Count your seeds. Which ones got past you?

ask.q: Real inspectors cannot check every bag on every ship. What would you do about that?
good: Ban the riskiest cargo, like soil.
Check hardest the ships from places with known weeds.
Watch the land near the harbour for the first newcomer.

flow.parent: Most children find 8 to 12 of the 15 seeds. The soil usually hides its seeds best. That is a true picture: parthenium probably reached India as seeds mixed in imported grain. Wash the dal before cooking.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Stowaway Check. Here you run your check against the clock and see which seeds got through.

worksheets.title: Why life lives where it does (core)

items.p: What does biogeography study?
opts: Where living beings are found, and why
items.why: Biogeography asks where each kind of living being is found, and why there and not somewhere else.

items.p: True or false: if a place suits an animal, that animal always lives there.
items.why: False. The animal's ancestors must also have been able to reach the place. The Arctic would probably suit penguins, but none live there.

items.p: Anything that stops a living being from spreading, such as a sea, is called a ____.
a: barrier
items.why: A barrier can be a sea, a mountain range, a desert or a change of climate. What counts as a barrier depends on the living being.

items.p: Match each traveller to the way they cross the sea.
items.why: Each traveller crosses in a way that suits their body. A coconut's husk is full of air, and a fern spore is as light as dust.

items.p: About how fast do the Earth's plates move?
items.why: Plates move a few centimetres a year, about as fast as a fingernail grows. Choosing 'they do not move' is natural, because nobody can feel it.

items.p: Put these in order, to tell India's journey.
items: India is joined to Madagascar inside Gondwana
The Seychelles break off from India
India moves north as an island
India meets Asia and the Himalaya rise
a: India is joined to Madagascar inside Gondwana
India splits from Madagascar
The Seychelles break off from India
India moves north as an island
India meets Asia and the Himalaya rise
items.why: India left Madagascar first and the Seychelles next. Then India crossed the sea alone, and last of all pushed into Asia.

items.p: Fossils of one land animal lie in India and in Antarctica. How could that be? Explain.
items.a: India and Antarctica were once joined in one land, Gondwana. The animal lived across that land. Later the land broke up and the pieces moved apart, carrying the fossils with them.
items.why: A strong answer says the lands were joined when the animal lived, and that the land moved afterwards. It does not need the animal to cross an ocean.

items.p: Why was the sea lower during the last ice age?
opts: The sea had dried in the Sun
Much water was frozen on the land
items.why: Thick ice lay on the land, and that water came from the sea. So the sea stood about 120 metres lower.

items.p: True or false: Sri Lanka was once joined to India by dry land.
items.why: True. The sea between them is very shallow. When the sea was lower, it was dry land, until about 7,000 years ago.

items.p: In the Separated Lines Test, why did the two mixed families stay close to each other?
items.a: Each new line in the mixed families was copied from both families. So a mistake in one family was shared with the other at the next step, and they could not drift apart.
items.why: A strong answer says that mixing shares every change between the two families. Careful copying is not the reason, because the copying was the same for all four.

items.p: A kind of living being found in only one place on Earth is ____ to that place.
a: endemic
items.why: Endemic means found naturally in one place and nowhere else. The Nicobar megapode is endemic to the Nicobar Islands.

items.p: Sort these. Are they native to India, or were they brought by people?
items.why: Neem, tigers and peafowl reached India without people. Chilli, lantana and potato all came from the Americas on ships.

items.p: What makes an introduced species 'invasive'?
opts: They spread alone and harm others
items.why: Invasive means brought by people, spreading without help and harming those who were there before. Coming from another country only makes a species introduced.

items.p: Lantana takes over forests in India but not in tropical America. What is one likely reason?
opts: The insects that eat lantana stayed behind
items.why: At home many insects and diseases feed on lantana. Most of them did not travel with the plant. This is one explanation, and scientists have others too.

items.p: Draw a mainland, an island near it and an island far away. Use arrows to show which island gets more travellers.
items.a: A mainland with many arrows reaching the near island and only one or two reaching the far island. The near island is drawn with more kinds of living beings on it.
items.why: A strong drawing shows fewer arrows reaching the far island, and so fewer kinds living there.
items.art: A blank box for a drawing.

items.p: Camels brought by people now live wild in Australia. What does that show about Australia before?
opts: It was too cold for camels
items.why: The land did not change when camels arrived. So it suited camels all along, and they were missing only because they could not get there.

items.p: A warm sea stops a penguin but not a sea turtle. Why does a barrier depend on who meets it?
items.a: A barrier is something a living being cannot cross. Penguins need cold water, so warm sea stops them. A sea turtle lives in warm sea, so for her it is a road.
items.why: A strong answer says that each living being has their own needs and ways of moving, so the same sea is a wall for one and a path for another.

items.p: Match each piece of evidence to what it shows.
pairs: The same fossils on two continents
Many DNA differences between two species
They have been apart a long time
Young rock along the middle of an ocean
New sea floor is forming there
Whole leaves on a newcomer plant
The insects that eat them may be missing
items.why: Each kind of evidence answers a different question: where the land was, how long ago a split happened, or what is happening now.

items.p: True or false: some of the heat that moves the plates comes from atoms breaking down deep underground.
items.why: True. About half of the Earth's inner heat comes from atoms of uranium, thorium and potassium breaking down. The rest is left from when the Earth formed.

items.p: Bali and Lombok are 35 kilometres apart, yet have very different animals. Why?
opts: Lombok is a much older island
The sea between them is deep
items.why: The channel is too deep to have become dry land in the ice age. Walking animals from Asia reached Bali and stopped there.

items.p: Draw the sea floor from a mainland to two islands, seen from the side. Label the three things listed.
labels: Sea level in the ice age
a: Shallow channel: between the mainland and the first island, above the ice-age sea level
Deep channel: between the two islands, still under water in the ice age
Sea level in the ice age: a line about 120 metres below today's sea level
items.why: A strong drawing shows the ice-age line below the shallow sea floor, so that it is dry, and above the deep sea floor, so that it stays sea.
items.art: A blank box for the child's own side view of a mainland and two islands, with three empty label lines.

items.p: The purple frog of Kerala has close relatives only on the Seychelles islands. Explain how that happened.
items.a: The land of India and the Seychelles was once joined. The frogs' ancestors lived on it. The land split about 65 million years ago, and the two groups of frogs changed separately ever since.
items.why: A strong answer has the land moving, and the frogs staying on it. Frogs cannot easily cross salt water, so swimming is not a good explanation.

items.p: Small mistakes made when DNA is copied are called ____.
a: mutations
mutation
items.why: A mutation is a small copying mistake in DNA. It is passed on to the young, and is one reason separated groups become different.

items.p: Sort these travellers. Are they likely or unlikely to reach a far island without people?
items.why: Fliers, floaters and wind-blown spores cross the sea. Salt water stops frogs and river fish, and an elephant cannot swim that far.

items.p: Why do far islands have many endemic species?
opts: Few arrive, and they stay isolated
items.why: Few living beings reach a far island, and their descendants do not mix with the mainland. Over a long time they become kinds found nowhere else.

items.p: A dry village in Tamil Nadu is covered with seemai karuvelam, an invasive thorn tree.

views.says: Remove every tree. They take scarce water from the ground and crowd out the native plants.
This tree is my income in a year without rain. Give us another living before you remove the trees.
Clear the trees round ponds and streams first, where they do most harm. Leave the rest for now.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason from the unit. Then answer one of the other views.
items.a: Any view with a reason. One reason is that an invasive tree harms native plants and uses water. Another is that people now depend on the tree. A good reply to another view says what that view gets right.
items.why: A strong answer uses a fact, such as the harm to native plants or the family's income, and treats the other view fairly.

items.p: True or false: every species that people bring to a new country becomes invasive.
items.why: False. Most introduced species, such as chilli and potato, grow only where people plant them. Only a few spread alone and do harm.

items.p: Put these steps of biological control in order.
items: Find an insect there who eats the invader
Test the insect on crops and native plants in closed cages
Release the insect only if they eat nothing else
Watch for years to see what happens
a: Find the invader's homeland
Find an insect there who eats the invader
Test the insect on crops and native plants in closed cages
Release the insect only if they eat nothing else
Watch for years to see what happens
items.why: The testing comes before the release, because a released insect cannot be called back.

items.p: Cane toads were released in Australia to eat beetles in sugarcane. What went wrong, and what test was missing?
items.a: The toads did not control the beetles. They multiplied into many millions, and their poison kills native animals who eat them. Nobody had first tested what the toads would eat and who would eat them.
items.why: A strong answer names both failures: the toads did not do the job, and they harmed others. It says the testing should have come before the release.

items.p: A bowl twice as far from scattering grains catches much less than half as many. Why?
opts: Rice is too heavy to bounce
The grains spread over a wider ring
items.why: Few grains travel far, and those that do are spread round a bigger circle. One bowl covers a smaller share of that circle.

worksheets.title: Evidence, deep time and hard choices (challenge)

items.p: Hummingbirds live only in the Americas, though India has many nectar flowers. Give two possible reasons.
items.a: One reason: hummingbirds arose in the Americas, and wide oceans stopped them reaching India. Another: India already has sunbirds who feed on nectar, so a newcomer would find the food taken.
items.why: A strong answer gives one reason about reaching the place, and one about what is already there. Both are possible, and a good answer says how to tell them apart.

items.p: A sea crossing happens about once in 10,000 years. About how many times in 1 million years?
items.why: 1,000,000 divided by 10,000 is 100. A crossing too rare for anyone to see becomes almost certain over a very long time.

items.p: Alfred Wegener said the continents had moved. Why did most geologists reject this? What later changed their minds?
items.a: Wegener could not say what force could move a continent, and nobody could feel the movement. Later, maps of the sea floor showed a long crack where new floor forms, and measurements showed the sea floor spreading.
items.why: A strong answer separates the two parts. The evidence of fit and fossils was there early. What was missing was a way for the land to move.

items.p: True or false: a plate moving 5 centimetres a year travels 50 kilometres in a million years.
items.why: True. 5 centimetres times 1,000,000 is 5,000,000 centimetres. That is 50,000 metres, which is 50 kilometres.

items.p: Two frog species differ in very many places in their DNA. What does that suggest?
opts: They have been apart a long time
They live in the same pond
items.why: Copying mistakes build up at a roughly steady rate. Many differences mean the two species have been separate for a long time.

items.p: Draw one group of birds split by a new sea. Then draw both groups a very long time later.
items.a: Two drawings. First: sea between two halves of a land, with the same birds on each side. Second: the birds on each side look different, for example in beak or colour.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the birds alike just after the split and different only much later. The sea does not change them. It stops them mixing.
items.art: A blank box for two drawings side by side.

items.p: Put these in order, from the atoms to the frogs.
items: Atoms deep in the Earth break down and give out heat
Hot rock in the mantle slowly flows
The plate carrying India moves away from Madagascar
Frogs on the two lands can no longer meet
The two groups of frogs become different families
a: Atoms deep in the Earth break down and give out heat
Hot rock in the mantle slowly flows
The plate carrying India moves away from Madagascar
Frogs on the two lands can no longer meet
The two groups of frogs become different families
items.why: Each step causes the next. Heat moves the rock, the rock helps to move the plates, the plates separate the land, and separation makes new kinds.

items.p: Lantana has grown in India's forests for about 200 years.

views.says: Remove the lantana. Grass cannot grow under the bushes, so deer and elephants lose their food.
Many birds now nest in lantana and eat the berries. Clearing all the bushes at once would hurt them.

views.who: A craftsperson who makes furniture from lantana
views.says: Cut the bushes and use the stems. They are strong, and the work pays for the clearing.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason. Then answer one of the other views.
items.a: Any view with a reason. Lantana does shade out grass. Birds do use the bushes. Cutting for craft does remove some. A good answer says where and how fast to clear, and what to plant afterwards.
items.why: A strong answer sees that all three views hold some truth, and proposes something that takes account of more than one.

items.p: Sri Lanka left India 7,000 years ago, and the Seychelles 65 million. Whose animals differ more from India's?
items.why: The longer two groups are kept apart, the more different they become. 65 million years is far longer than 7,000.

items.p: The common myna is native in India and invasive in Australia. Explain how one bird can be both.
items.a: Native and invasive describe a species in a place. Mynas reached India without people, so they are native here. People took them to Australia, where they spread and drive native birds from their nest holes.
items.why: A strong answer says that the words belong to the bird and the place together. The bird is the same in both countries.

items.p: Sort these clues. Does each point to missing enemies, or to land that people disturbed?
items: No insect in the new land eats the plant
The plant's diseases stayed at home
An insect brought from home controls the plant
The forest was cut and burned first
The plant fills a newly cleared roadside
items.why: Both causes are real, and they often work together. Knowing which matters more tells people what to do about it.

items.p: True or false: a species who arrived 10,000 years ago without people counts as native.
items.why: True. Native means arriving, or arising, without being carried by people. How long ago does not matter.

items.p: In the last ice age, sea less than about ____ metres deep became dry land.
items.why: The sea level fell about 120 metres, so any sea floor shallower than that was uncovered.

items.p: Some scientists think a planet needs moving plates to have many kinds of life. What evidence would help test this?
items.a: We would need other planets to compare: some with moving plates and some without. If life, or varied life, were found only on planets with plates, that would support the idea. With one living planet we cannot tell.
items.why: A strong answer sees that one example cannot test the idea, and says what a comparison would need.

items.p: Why do introduced rats harm island birds more than mainland birds?
opts: Island birds never met hunting mammals
items.why: On many far islands no hunting mammal ever arrived. Birds there nest on the ground and do not flee. They have no defence against a rat.

quiz.p: Polar bears do not live in Antarctica. What is the most likely reason?
opts: Their ancestors could not reach it
quiz.why: Polar bears arose in the far north, and no land or ice ever joined the north to Antarctica. Antarctica is cold and has seals, so it might well suit them.

quiz.p: Which of these is a barrier for a river fish?
opts: A deep pool in the river
quiz.why: A river fish lives in fresh water. Salt water and dry land both stop a river fish spreading to the next river.

quiz.p: How can a young spider cross many kilometres of sea?
opts: Carried by wind on a silk thread
quiz.why: A young spider lets out a thread of silk, and the wind lifts thread and spider together. This is how spiders reach new islands so early.

opts: A giant southern land that broke apart
quiz.why: Gondwana was a huge southern land. Its pieces are now Africa, South America, Antarctica, Australia, Madagascar and India.

quiz.p: True or false: India has always been joined to Asia.
quiz.why: False. India was part of Gondwana, then an island, and began to join Asia only about 50 million years ago.

quiz.p: What can turn a shallow sea into a land bridge?
opts: The sea level falling in an ice age
quiz.why: In an ice age much water is frozen on land, so the sea falls. Shallow sea floor is uncovered and joins two lands.

quiz.p: A sea splits one species into two groups. What happens over a very long time?
quiz.why: Each group makes its own small changes, and nothing mixes them. Choosing 'nothing changes' forgets that every copy of DNA has a few mistakes.

quiz.p: Which island will probably have the fewest kinds of living beings?
opts: A small island far from land
A large island far from land
quiz.why: Few travellers reach a far island, and a small island keeps fewer kinds alive. Small and far together give the fewest.

quiz.p: Potato plants came to India from South America and grow only on farms. They are:
quiz.why: People brought potatoes, so they are introduced. They do not spread through wild land or harm others, so they are not invasive.

quiz.p: Before releasing an insect to control a weed, what must scientists test?
opts: That the insect lives for years
That the insect is easy to see
That the insect eats only that weed
quiz.why: An insect who also eats crops or native plants would become a new problem. Cane toads in Australia were released without such a test.

quiz.p: A water weed doubles every two weeks. When is the weed cheapest to remove?
opts: When the whole lake is covered
When the first few plants appear
When half the lake is covered
quiz.why: A few plants can be lifted out by hand. A half-covered lake is only two weeks from being full, and then the work is enormous.

quiz.p: Which is the best evidence that two lands were once joined?
opts: The same land-animal fossils on both
quiz.why: A land animal could not cross an ocean, so matching fossils point to joined land. Weather and rivers can be alike on lands that never touched.

applications: Plant quarantine at airports and ports. Officers check plants, seeds, soil and fruit that travellers and ships bring, so that new weeds and insects are stopped at the border.
Rules for ships. A ship carries sea water in tanks for balance and lets it out at the next port. Ships must now treat this water, because it carries tiny sea animals round the world.
Biological control. India's bureau for farm insects in Bengaluru tests natural enemies of weeds and pests before they are released.
Finding coal. Geologists look for coal in India in rocks of the same age as the coal of Australia and South Africa, because those lands were once joined.
Earthquake maps. Engineers use the measured movement of the Indian plate to decide how strong buildings must be in the Himalaya and the North-East.
Planning protected areas. A patch of forest surrounded by farms is like an island. Planners join such patches with strips of forest so that animals can keep mixing.

Tracing a new pest. In 2018 a caterpillar from the Americas who eats maize was first found in India, in Karnataka. Scientists compared the moths' DNA with moths from other countries, to trace where they had come from.

open_questions.q: When exactly did India first touch Asia?
open_questions.why_open: Different kinds of rock evidence give dates from about 55 million to about 35 million years ago. Some scientists think there were two meetings, a soft one and then a hard one.

open_questions.q: How did the first monkeys cross from Africa to South America?
open_questions.why_open: Most scientists think they rode a raft of plants across an ocean that was narrower then. Nobody has found direct evidence of the crossing, and it must have taken many days without fresh water.

open_questions.q: Why does lantana spread so much more in India than at home?
open_questions.why_open: Missing enemies, disturbed forests, the plant's own chemicals and many separate plantings have all been suggested. The share of each has not been measured.

open_questions.q: When did the Earth's plates first begin to move?
open_questions.why_open: Estimates run from more than 3 billion years ago to less than 1 billion. The oldest rocks have been melted and remade, so the evidence is thin.

open_questions.q: As the climate warms, can living beings move to new places as fast as their climate moves?
open_questions.why_open: Some birds and insects are already shifting their ranges. Slow travellers such as trees and frogs may not keep up, and roads and farms now stand in their way.

maths.problem: In a Separated Lines Test, the gap between families A and B was 7, 17, 19, 29 and 31 millimetres at generations 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10. The gap between the mixed families C and D was 2, 3, 3, 3 and 2. Describe each pattern. What would you expect at generation 20?
maths.answer: The gap between A and B grows, by about 3 millimetres a generation. The gap between C and D stays at 2 or 3 millimetres. At generation 20, A and B would probably be about 60 millimetres apart, and C and D still about 3.
maths.explain: From generation 2 to generation 10 the A and B gap rose from 7 to 31. That is 24 millimetres in 8 generations, or 3 a generation. Ten more generations would add about 30, giving about 60. The C and D gap shows no rise at all. The prediction for A and B is rough, because the gap grows by chance steps and not by a fixed rule.
maths.context: This is about the Separated Lines Test. Two families of lines are copied apart, and two are mixed at each step. These are made-up results.

chart.title: Made-up results: the gap between two families (millimetres)
cols: Gap between A and B (kept apart)

maths.why_maths: One row of a table can mislead. Looking at how a number changes down the whole table shows whether a gap is growing or only wobbling.

maths.problem: A thumbnail grows about 3.5 millimetres a month. The Indian plate moves about 5 centimetres a year. Which is faster?
maths.answer: The Indian plate, by a little. The nail grows about 4.2 centimetres a year, and India moves 5.
maths.explain: First put both in the same units. 3.5 millimetres a month times 12 months is 42 millimetres a year. 42 millimetres is 4.2 centimetres. 5 centimetres is more than 4.2 centimetres. So the land under your feet moves a little faster than your nail grows.
maths.context: In Your Nail and India you measure how fast your thumbnail grows, and compare it with the movement of the Indian plate.
maths.why_maths: Two speeds can be compared only when both use the same length and the same time.

maths.problem: The Indian plate moves about 5 centimetres a year. How far does it move in 1 million years? How long does it take to move 1 kilometre?
maths.answer: 50 kilometres in 1 million years. 1 kilometre takes 20,000 years.
maths.explain: 5 centimetres times 1,000,000 is 5,000,000 centimetres. Divide by 100 to get 50,000 metres, and by 1,000 to get 50 kilometres. For 1 kilometre: 1 kilometre is 100,000 centimetres, and 100,000 divided by 5 is 20,000 years. A speed too slow to see covers the width of an ocean in 100 million years.
maths.context: The Earth's plates carry the continents a few centimetres every year. This problem shows how such a slow movement adds up.
maths.why_maths: Nobody can watch a continent move. Multiplying a small yearly step by a very large number of years shows what the movement does in the end.

maths.problem: In Clear the Tank, a weed covers 1 square of 64 and doubles every round. Nobody clears the weed. After how many rounds is the tank full? In which round was it half full? One round is two weeks. How many weeks of warning does a half-full tank give?
maths.answer: Full after 6 rounds. Half full after 5 rounds. A half-full tank gives only 2 weeks of warning.
maths.explain: Keep doubling: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64. That is 6 doublings, so 6 rounds, which is 12 weeks. Half of 64 is 32, which comes one round before the end. So when the tank is half covered, only one round, or 2 weeks, is left.
maths.context: In Clear the Tank you play a water weed that doubles every round on a grid of 64 squares.
maths.why_maths: Doubling starts slowly and ends fast. Working out the numbers shows why an invasive weed must be cleared while there are still very few plants.

maths.problem: In a Far Island Test, 2,100 grains of rice were poured in three pours. The near bowl caught 54, the middle bowl 9 and the far bowl 1. What fraction of the near bowl's catch did the middle bowl get? Was 'twice as far' the same as 'half as many'?
maths.answer: One sixth. No: twice as far gave one sixth as many, not one half.
maths.explain: 9 divided by 54 is one sixth. If distance worked simply, the middle bowl would have caught half of 54, which is 27. It caught far fewer. Fewer grains bounce that far, and those that do are spread round a wider ring of floor. Notice also that only 64 grains of the 2,100 reached any island. Most travellers land in the sea.
maths.context: This is about the Far Island Test. Rice is poured onto an upturned bowl, and bowls at three distances catch the scattered grains. These are made-up results.
maths.why_maths: A fraction turns three separate counts into one comparison, and tests the guess that twice as far means half as many.

maths.problem: Suppose a storm carries a lizard alive to a certain far island about once in every 10,000 years. How many arrivals would you expect in 1 million years? How many in your own 10 years of life?
maths.answer: About 100 arrivals in 1 million years. In 10 years, about one thousandth of an arrival, which means almost certainly none.
maths.explain: 1,000,000 divided by 10,000 is 100. For 10 years: 10 divided by 10,000 is one thousandth. So nobody alive is likely to see it happen, and yet over a million years it happens about a hundred times. The figure of once in 10,000 years is made up, to show the reasoning.
maths.context: Animals sometimes reach islands on floating trees after storms. Such crossings are very rare. This problem asks what 'very rare' means over a very long time.
maths.why_maths: People judge what is possible by what they have seen. Dividing the time by the rarity shows that a thing nobody has seen can still be almost certain.
