how_we_found_out.context: How did people find out that the continents move, and carry living beings with them? This card tells the true story, and the idea that turned out wrong.
how_we_found_out.story: Fossils of the same land animals lie in India, Africa and Antarctica. For a long time geologists explained this with land bridges: strips of land that once joined the continents and later sank under the sea. In 1864 Philip Sclater even proposed a whole sunken land, which he named Lemuria. In 1912 Alfred Wegener, a German weather scientist, said the continents themselves had been joined and had moved apart. Most geologists rejected this, because he could not say what could move a continent. He died in Greenland in 1930. In 1952 Marie Tharp was drawing the floor of the Atlantic from ships' depth readings. Women were not then allowed on the research ships. She found a deep valley running along an undersea mountain range, as if the sea floor were splitting there. Her colleague Bruce Heezen called it 'girl talk'. Then a map of undersea earthquakes was laid over her drawing, and the earthquakes followed her valley. In the 1960s other measurements showed new sea floor forming along it. No sunken bridges were ever found.
how_we_found_out.who: Alfred Wegener, who proposed that continents move. Marie Tharp, who mapped the ocean floor and found the rift valley, with Bruce Heezen, who collected the depth readings at sea. Philip Sclater, who proposed the sunken land of Lemuria.
how_we_found_out.when: 1864 (Sclater's Lemuria), 1912 (Wegener's lecture), 1952 (Tharp finds the rift valley), 1957 (her first map is published) and the 1960s (moving plates accepted)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That the continents have always been where they are, and that land bridges once joined them and then sank. Maps of the sea floor found no sunken bridges. They found a crack where new sea floor forms and pushes the continents apart.
how_we_found_out.art: A woman at a large drawing table in the 1950s inking a map of undersea mountains with a deep valley down the middle, and a globe beside her.

roots.context: In this unit you copied lines, fitted continents together and met plants that crossed an ocean with people. Here we ask what it means that living beings become different when they are kept apart.

deep_truth.truth: In the Separated Lines Test, four families of lines began as copies of one 100 millimetre line. You copied every line as carefully as you could. The two families kept apart still ended at different lengths, and the two that mixed stayed close. So living beings who are kept apart become different, and those who keep mixing stay alike. A sea between them is enough, given a very long time.
deep_truth.habit: When the animals of an island differ from those of the mainland, we ask what the island did to them. The test points another way. The separated copies became different with nothing done to them. They were only kept apart. So the first thing to look for is the barrier.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Separated Lines Test the copier, the pencil and the care were the same for all four families, and only the mixing differed. Leopards in India and Sri Lanka have been apart for about 7,000 years and still look alike. The purple frog and her Seychelles relatives have been apart for about 65 million years and look nothing alike.

three.who_am_i: You belong to one human species because people have never stopped mixing. Humans spread to every continent, but travellers kept meeting and having children together.
three.what_is_life: Life copies itself, and no copy is perfect. So wherever a barrier holds two groups apart, life becomes two kinds.
three.what_is_this_world: The ground is not fixed. The land you live on has crossed an ocean, and it still moves about 5 centimetres every year.

roots.thread: All living beings on Earth share one ancestor. From that one beginning came millions of kinds. This unit shows one way it happened. Moving plates, rising seas and rare journeys kept splitting groups apart, and each separated group went on changing by itself. So the many kinds of life are one family that has been divided again and again. When people carry a plant across an ocean, they undo in a few weeks a separation that lasted millions of years.

teachings.teaching: The poet says that every town is his town and every person is his kin. He says life makes its way like a raft on a great river in flood, carried where the water takes it.
teachings.link: The poet was speaking of people. It meets this unit's science in two plain ways. Many living beings are where they are because a current, a wind or a moving land carried their ancestors there. And all living beings are one family, so each one is kin to the rest.

teachings.teaching: The Buddha says that all things that are put together pass away, and that seeing this clearly leads to peace.
teachings.link: A continent seems the most lasting thing there is. Yet Gondwana broke into pieces, and the sea between India and Sri Lanka was dry land 7,000 years ago. Here the science agrees with the verse: lands, seas and kinds of living beings all change.

science.text: All living beings on Earth share one ancestor. Every one of them uses the same DNA code.
The Earth's plates are moving now. Satellites measure the movement, which is a few centimetres a year.
Some scientists think a planet needs moving plates to have many kinds of life. With only one living planet to study, nobody can test this yet.

other_view.who: Daniel Simberloff, an American ecologist, and many conservation scientists
other_view.view: Every species is descended from travellers, and that is true. But a species that has lived in a place for a million years has neighbours who eat them and limits that hold them in check. A species carried there last year has none. So 'native' is a real and useful word. Treating every arrival alike would excuse great harm, most of all on islands.

practice.title: One minute on moving ground
practice.say: Sit on the floor and put both palms flat on it. Close your eyes. The floor feels still. But this land is moving north-east, about as fast as your thumbnail grows. Breathe in and out slowly, five times. With each breath, think of the land sliding a tiny way, with you and your home on it. Now open your eyes. Who else is riding on this piece of land with you?
practice.kid: Sit with both palms flat on the floor. Close your eyes. The land is moving as slowly as a nail grows. Breathe slowly five times. Open your eyes. Who else rides on this land?

ask: Tigers walked into India long ago, and lantana was carried here 200 years ago. Is there a real difference between arriving and being brought?
Languages also drift apart when two groups of people stop talking to each other. Is that the same thing that happened to your lines?
The land under you has moved thousands of kilometres. So where is 'here'?

playtest: Read through as a parent and child in a city flat would use it, step by step. The experiments were reasoned through carefully but not yet tried at home, so treat the amounts as a starting point. The Separated Lines Test (core) needs only four sheets of paper, a pencil, a ruler and a folded newspaper. It takes 35 to 40 minutes, and a child can do it alone. In most runs the two separated families should end 10 to 40 millimetres apart, and the two mixed families less than 10 millimetres apart. Because the changes are chance steps, the separated families will sometimes end close together. A computer run of the same rules, with copying mistakes of 4 to 10 millimetres, gave the expected result in about four runs out of five. The last step says what to do then: count the rows, or run a third family. Who Lives Where (core) needs a world map to copy from. The Gondwana Jigsaw (core) needs thin paper and a map. Paper continents fit only roughly, and Antarctica must be drawn as an oval, because flat maps stretch it. The Far Island Test puts rice on a clean bedsheet. How far the grains bounce depends on the floor and the height, so the first step is a trial pour to place the bowls. The far bowl may catch nothing, and that is a fair result. The rice can be washed and cooked. Land Bridge in a Tray uses atta dough, which goes soft in water after about 15 minutes. Your Nail and India gives a gap of only 1 to 2 millimetres in two weeks, so measure in good light. Count the Bites needs plants outdoors and is not in the core path. Its result can go either way, and the unit says so. Facts looked up while writing: the dates of Wegener, Tharp and Sclater. The numbers for the Wallace Line and the ice-age sea level. The depth of the sea between India and Sri Lanka. The break-up of Gondwana and the speed of the Indian plate. The share of the Earth's heat from radioactive atoms. Krakatau, the Anguilla iguanas, the lemurs' crossing and the globe skimmer dragonfly. The wallabies in New Zealand. The 1967 island theory and the mangrove island test. The 2011 exchange in Nature. The homelands and arrival dates of lantana, water hyacinth, parthenium, the giant African snail, seemai karuvelam and salvinia. Cane toads, the mongoose in Jamaica and the myna in Australia. Nail growth. The two teachings. All three video addresses were confirmed with YouTube, but the videos were not watched. Four things could not be confirmed from a second source, so a person should check them: the year chital were taken to the Andaman Islands, the court orders on seemai karuvelam, the view given for Praveen Karanth, and the exact year the salvinia weevil was released in Kerala (sources give 1982 or 1983).
